to put a bit of context around these changes, because there has been a lot of noise and a
lot of, well, squawking—I think that seems to be the word of the day for them—around
this. So the context around th e changes: currently, if you study at the universities the
Crown pays 70c in every dollar;  70 percent of course costs are already paid for by the
2814 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
taxpayer, by the Crown. We ha ve interest-free student loans.  They are available to all
who choose to study—undergraduate or postgra duate. We also know that, effectively,
between 40c and 50c in every dollar has to be written off on those student loans, a
further cost—or a gift, if you like, of the Crown to those who are choosing to study.
We also know that there are a multitude of  scholarships available to students from
the private sector and from the public sector . I note that the Prime Minister’s Science
Prizes were announced yesterda y. So, already, we have a picture here of the generosity
of the Crown, the generosity of the taxpaye rs to people who choos e to study. As I said,
70c in every dollar goes towards their studies;  interest-free student loans, a significant
write-down on that; scholarships; and, of c ourse, we still have 200 weeks of student
allowance for those in undergraduate degr ees, including those who choose to do
honours. But I am aware that people are not happy, and I have to sa y, particularly to
those students who are unhappy, I find that the generosity of the ta xpayer really is
nothing short of astonishing. If you look at it in that context, the giving that the taxpayer
provides is nothing short of astonishing. But, of course, some people are still not happy.

items.speaker: Jacinda Ardern
items.text: Is education a public good? Is it a public good, Simon?
SIMON O’CONNOR : And although I cannot fully he ar the interjections, I am
aware that some people are still not happy, because you real ise there are about 20,000
people in this country who are doing mast ers or postgraduate de grees. That is 0.5
percent of the population. And what is being asked for here, in the complaints around
this Budget to do with tertiary  education, is that the 0.5 pe rcent want more: they want
more than 70 percent of their fees paid, they want more than 200 weeks of allowance,
they want more than an interest-free student loan, they want more than the scholarships,
they want more than the opportunities. As we well know, for most who do postgraduate
studies there is opportunity to  earn money through their teaching and tutorials, and so
forth. I say this not just as someone who speaks in theory but someone who has done
two postgraduate degrees. I am very consci ous that you do this freely and through a
choice. For the record, I did my first postgraduate degree while working full-time and
studying part-time, because I was aware of th e financial consideration. And, just to add
to it, because I recall the Green Party ma king an emotional but empty series of
statements, when I did my second postgradua te degree, I was doing that working full-
time and studying full-time. You see, education is a choice, and choices can be made,
and I for one as a postgraduate student have appreciated what the Crown has done.
As I wrap up I would like to say that in theory I would wish that everything was free.
It would be great. But that is not the world that we live in. Only in Labour do they think
that everything should be free. I am consci ous we are only a few weeks away from the
mid-winter Christmas, if you like, and Labour does have a Christmas list that is a mile
long. But Santa is not going to pay for the bi lls and the gifts that Labour wants to give
away, because in the real world we understand  that grown-ups have to pay the bill. So
we are not going to allow Labour to have people sit on its lap and demand gift after gift,
because it is ultimately the taxpayer who is going to groan and pay the bill.

items.speaker: I come back to where I started
items.text: this is a sensible Budget. It is a Budget for its time. I
am proud of the decisions that have been ma de. I am proud of the decisions that have
been made in education, and particularly in the tertiary sector. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker.
That was the member for T āmaki, Simon O’Connor, who was happy to support the loss
of teachers in intermediates in  his electorate. He is stan ding in front of this House
promoting education and what the Government has done. National has framed its fourth
Budget as a zero Budget, but a zero Budget is about zero hope, zero aspiration, and zero
opportunity for the hard-working Kiwis strugg ling to make a living. They deserve more
from a Budget than the one National dished out.
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2815
We know that 13 days is a very, very, very  long time in politics. The Minister of
Education stood up in this House during the Budget debate promoting great gains in
education. Just 13 days later she had to not  only retract but re verse and do a whole
about-face on a policy that fundamentally im pacted on children and parents in the
delivery of education as people know it and want  to preserve it in their communities. It
was an epic blunder that needed to be fi xed, and Labour members were happy that we
raised those questions in th e House to assure good-thinki ng New Zealanders that we
were working with them on this issue.
The Minister claimed that the Government  was focusing on quali ty, not quantity, in
the form of the new staff ratios that it wa nted to introduce, ca pping teacher numbers
over the next 4-year period. Well, it simply did not stack up. As people worked through
the detail and as we presented questions in th e House to the Minister  that could not be
answered, more and more red flags went up as bastions of opposition in the schools and
in our communities by parents who believe that their children deserve more. Parents
were furious at the prospect that losing one or two teachers would fundamentally impact
on the learning of their children. Why? Because they translated the National
Government’s changes as la rger class sizes, fewer teach ers, and less opportunity for
their children to get a really good chance in the classroom for one-on-one feedback from
their teachers. They knew that it just did not make sense.
The Minister talked a big game, but she was short on detail. This became more and
more evident as we started to understand th e real effects of th e policy that she was
presenting to the House in Budget 2012. When she came to this House and introduced
the fact that for years 7 and 8 technology te achers would be included in the new staff
ratios, we were flabbergasted on this side  of the House. Immediately, members on this
side of the House were getting calls from intermediate schools saying: “She’s got it
wrong. We’re not losing just two teachers; we could be losing up to eight teachers.”
And that is not just about technology teach ers; it is about delivering subjects like
science, like art, like drama, like all sorts of technology subjects, like kapahaka, and like
gifted learning. Then we had a whole lot of primary schools saying: “Well, actually, for
our young learners it may mean a cut to the extent that we cannot deliver remedial
maths or recovery reading to our youngest le arners, who are often the ones who need it
most.”
The Minister still stood in this Chamber an d defended that policy to members on this
side of the House as if it was a great ga in in education, and we knew it was not. We
knew that, fundamentally, children would mi ss out. Well, hello! It was not until the
adjournment, when members of the Government went back into their own communities,
that they were flooded with very angry National supporters who said, time and time
again, that the Government had it wrong. Thirteen days later, right up until the end, the
Minister was still defending this polic y. One morning she was saying that the
Government was not going to reverse the polic y, the next minute she was saying that it
would make a partial retraction, and then by day 13 she said it would reverse this
policy. The heat was too hot, and she knew that the Government had got it wrong.

items.speaker: Let me ask this
items.text: did the Minister, in fact, ask for the necessary information of
officials to ensure that prior to making th is decision the Government had got all the
information it needed to assure  itself that it was not goi ng to fundamentally impact on
the delivery of education in the communities? If she did ask for the information, did
Cabinet override that advice? We have not had any answers on that front. Or did she
deliberately ignore that information? Ti me and time again, when we were asking
questions of the Minister in this House on that pa rticular issue, sh e managed to evade
some detail on some very important questions.

items.speaker: Maggie Barry
items.text: Listen to the answers.
2816 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012

items.speaker: Hon NANAIA MAHUTA
items.text: But parents deserve an answer. Parents deserve an
answer. That member should be listening to constituents in her own electorate, who
were equally as angry on this particular i ssue. That member wa s happy to go out and
promote a policy that would fundamentally s ee the loss of teacher s in intermediate
schools in many electorates throughout the country.
Labour said it would reverse this ridiculous policy, beca use it did not stack up.
Putting more children into a class and more pressure on a teacher to teach those children
and give quality feedback would cause only more stress, and National was not listening
to them. We did. We said very early on in the piece that we would reverse it.
The Minister needs to spell out her plan about how National will invest in quality
teaching, because this is an important aspi ration. It should be done. But now that the
Government has reversed the policy on larger  class sizes, I ask whether it will retract
from its investments in improving the quality of teaching. There is no answer. Not a
word. Not a sigh. Not anything. Members on that  side of the House have their heads
down. Continuing to invest in quality teaching, we believe, is an important thing to do,
but the Minister will need to demonstr ate where she will now find savings from,
because that particular investment is essential.
The other part of the humiliating reversal that she had to do and backtrack on was
really supported by the words of young people themselves. I suspect that once the anger
of parents moved into the domain of suppor tive evidence from teachers and then was
translated through children, they started to  get upset about the prospect of losing
technology teachers. This is how they explained it at Kōwhai Intermediate School: “The
good thing about technology classes is that th ey’re a fun way to learn things that you
may need to do when you’re older.” They also said: “In primary schools they don’t
offer technology.” and “Creativity and prac tical skills are an important part of
education.” But here is the point that I think National me mbers might want to hear.

items.speaker: Students at Kōwhai Intermediate School said
items.text: “Getti ng good grades in other subjects is
important, but people who make a difference in  the world usually have a unique way of
looking at things. You cannot be one of these people without creativity, and that is what
technology classes deliver.” He re is a Government that says, on the one hand, that it
wants a brighter future for all New Zealande rs, but then it cuts technology teachers in
our intermediate schools and limits the opportunity for our children to be able to take up
courses that teach creative innovation. Th e Government got it wrong. We are happy to
see the reversal.
There are so many other areas in which things do not add up. We see increased
funding for private schools since 2009—$14 million extra every year since National has
come into Government. What is happening there? In last year’s Budget $21.8 million
went into public-private partnership business case modelling, and we still have not got
any detail on exactly how much has been  spent on the Hobsonville public-private
partnership project. In adult and community education a fu rther $4 million has been cut
from universities, affecting th eir ability to offer things like language programmes and
computer skills. Here is a Government th at is cut, cut, cutting and limiting the
opportunities in a whole lot of areas for people to continue to thrive in education.
Finally, I will respond to the member for T āmaki, who talked about student
allowances. We do believe on this side of  the House that postgraduate study is
important. Limiting access to a student allowance to only 200 weeks will affect those
who cannot afford to go into postgraduate study. We will see a lo t of people who are
unable to take up the opportunity to continue  to improve their skills because of a
decision that this Government  has made. We do not support it. The fourth Budget for
National has got it wrong in education. Nati onal should be ashamed about what it was
proposing to do, pulling the wool over parents’ eyes. Parents are not stupid. We are glad
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2817
we supported them on that fundamental issue of giving our children the very best in
education. Kia ora.

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: I must say that was an awfully long
10 minutes. I thought about taki ng a point of order and ques tioning whether or not the
clock had stopped, but everybody is allowed to have their say in  Parliament, and that is
a marvellous thing.
This is a great Budget, particularly when one looks around the world and sees what is
happening elsewhere. When we look around we  often like to compare ourselves with
Australia. Of course, in Australia they do mi ning and resources—the sorts of things the
Opposition would not have us touch, but it is happy to take the income that comes from
them. But, actually, what this Budget has been  able to do is to continue down the great
path that the National-led Government, along with our co lleagues in the ACT Party,
United Future, and the Māori Party, has been able to deliver.
I look at the law and order and justice areas—and they are the ones that I am most
concerned with—and at what we  have seen in a time when there has been a global
financial crisis and a recession. We came into  Government and the country had been in
recession for the last three quarters. We were told that what would happen is that there
would be an increase in crime, that crime would go up, that we woul d run out of prison
beds, and that we would be in a terrible situation. And we came in and we found that
there had been these new prisons built by the previous Labour Government—and they
are extremely flash, I have to say; extremel y flash—but it needed a lot of work to put
those double bunks in, and that seemed to sort out quite a few of our issues.
Then, of course, we brought in a pr ivate prison—private management—which
seems to be fantastic, really—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: How many people have escaped from it?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: The member over there, Mr  Hipkins, seems to have
forgotten that there were two escapes from Waikeria Prison just the other day, which, of
course, is State run. Of cour se, in the private sector wh en one of Serco’s prisoners
escapes it costs them $150,000. But nobody pays in the public sector.
What we have seen is actually a situation where the crime rate has come down. It is
now at the same level as it was in 1982—1982—and in amongst all of that we have also
seen the prison population start to fall in a sustained way for the first time since the
1930s. So instead of Labour, which was consta ntly having to catch up with more prison
beds, this Government has got the situation where we have now announced the closure
of two prisons, Wellington’s Mt Crawford  prison and New Plymouth Prison, which
should never have been used for housing pe ople in today’s world. We would not have
had to use them if we had b een left with enough beds by the previous Government. But
anyway, those are just some of the success stories.
We can also say there are 600 more police on the beat—600 more  front-line police.
There is now DNA testing for serious offenders, and ther e are tools to seize the
proceeds of crime. That has been a great success. Serious criminals and repeat offenders
are being kept behind bars longer with no bail  or parole eligibility. It was this party—
this party—along with our co alition partners United Futu re and the ACT Party that
brought through the Search and Surveillance Act, which should have been done years
ago. It was first started in about 2007, but, unfortunately, so me parties in this House
decided they were going to play politics with  this most important issue and were quite
happy to leave the police out there unable to  deal with methamphetamine dealers and
the like. Shame on them for not taking the right stance.
What we have seen, though, in amongst all of that is this Prime Minister take on the
role of saying that he wanted  to tackle methamphetamine in this country, and he has
done so with outstanding results. He has ma de sure that departments have worked
2818 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
together and that Ministers have worked together, and th ere has been a coordinated
approach. So instead of the previous Labour Government’s approach of saying: “Oh, we
can’t do anything about it, because it might upset their rights.” or some other nonsense
like that, what we have seen is coordinated work across the police, the Customs Service,
justice, health, and the prison sy stem to make sure we deal with this issue. We are now
starting to see some really good  improvement, but the battle is still not over. There is
still more work to do.
We have also seen the road toll come down to the lowest it has been in 50 years, and
that is about very smart road policing. It is  also about new road safety initiatives and
better public awareness as well,  so congratulations to all those people involved in that;
they have made us very proud. We have ha d 18 new public safety laws passed, we have
over 6,000 families now protected by police safe ty orders, we have got prison escapes
actually at the lowest levels ever, and we have 2,000 victims now supported through the
offender levy—and, yes, there is more.
Under this Budget what we are seeing is  not what we are seeing in many other
similar countries around the world, which are seeing massive redundancies in police and
massive loss of confidence in the safety of  the public. We are actually seeing the police
maintained at the level they have been at. Ye s, they are constantly looking at how they
can use technology to upgrade the way in which they work to be smarter, faster, and
more effective in preventing crime in the fi rst place. They have brought in the Policing
Excellence programme, which has been a fa ntastic success, and it is going to keep
going.
In addition, in the Ministry of Justice in particular we are looking at the work we are
doing across the sector to make sure that we look at the “crime lines”, you could say, of
those coming in through the pipeline, those coming into the justice system either in
youth justice or elsewhere and ending up in the prison and probation area. What we are
doing is that the Ministers are working together  to make sure that what we do, and what
our chief executives do, is constantly pred icated on the need to bring crime further
down, to bring youth crime down, and to bring down violent assaults. So this is better
public service. This is actually about looking at how we can better manage the resources
we have, how we can better react to the pub lic, and how we can be smart in how we
operate.
Coming up this year will be a completion of the review of the Family Court, and that
is something that I am very passionate about, having practised for around 20 years,
some of it in the family area. I have seen  over the years many times when the Family
Court has been used to abuse others, when children have not been put at the forefront of
parents’ minds—sorry, my throat is going.

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: You wouldn’t be emotional?

items.speaker: Hon JUDITH COLLINS
items.text: No, definitely not. But what we have seen, actually, is a
situation where children can be used by one parent to attack the other, and that is simply
not acceptable. The State should not fund that sort of behaviour; the State should not be
complicit in it. The State should be better than that, and that is what we expect to be.
In tertiary education we are continuing to target student assistance to where it is most
needed and ensure better value for taxpa yers. Simon O’Connor spoke about his two
postgraduate degrees, both completed when he was working full-time and studying full-
time. I feel like I could say that I sort of did the same too: in my first postgraduate
degree, working full-time and studying part- time, and in my second, working full-time
and studying part-time. It is hard to do it th at way, but at the end of the day we did not
owe anyone any money at the en d of it. It is a tough road, but that is what happens. I
think we have to be very careful what we do in tertiary education. We also have to be
very careful with taxpayers’ money. We also have to understand that the people who are
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2819
the panel beaters and the people who work in the supermarkets expect us to be careful
with their tax money as well, and expect a decent return for it, and that means good
education, good outcomes, and people contributing to the economy.
In essence and in conclusion, this is an  excellent Budget, given very difficult
financial times around the world. We just have to look at our friends  in Europe to see
what has happened there, and we are not just talking about Greece. There are other parts
of Europe that are very badly affected, and not just Europe: the UK, parts of Australia,
and parts of the United States. Some have  been going through very, very tough times,
much tougher than ours. We are very fortunate in where we are placed in the world, we
are very fortunate to have a judicial system that is not corrupt, and we are very fortunate
to have a police force that is not corrupt. All these things help to build confidence in the
economy and confidence in business. However, we are a small country and we have to
live within our means, and this Budget does.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: There are a couple of things that the
Minister of Justice, who has just resumed her seat, forgot  to mention. Sure, the crime
rate has come down. Perhaps that had so mething to do, Mrs Collins, with the 1,000
extra police officers on the front line that th e Labour-led Government  put on in its last
term in office. Perhaps it had something to  do with totally re vamping the thoroughly
inadequate, rundown prison system that we inherited from the last National
Government. Perhaps it had something to do w ith the total overhaul of legislation for
the Sentencing Act, the Parole Act, and the Proceeds of Crime Act. Perhaps it had
something to do with that.
But what Mrs Collins has not told us is what this Budget is doing for policing. This

items.speaker: Budget represents a real cut to police funding
items.text: 125 staffing positions cut, and that is just
to begin with. Dozens of police stations, Mrs Collins, will close during this term. Do
you know what I found out about my local police station? I found out that they might
not close it, but they will close it to the publ ic. They will close the police station to the
public. What does that mean for community po licing? I was standing there talking to a
member of the police force who is also on the local community board when a woman
biked up in distress and said that she had been sexually threatened by a man just down
the road. In future, do you know what she will have to do? She will have to bike to
Avondale. That is 9 kilometres away. Do you think she is going to report that crime? Do
you think the police are going to be able to respond immediately to it? Not on your life.
Police stations, mark my words,  will close in their dozens, and that is the very opposite
of what community policing is meant to be about. Then the Police Association told my
colleague Kris Faafoi here that the Govern ment is going to cut the pay of front-line
police officers over the next 10 years—it is going to cut it. The previous Minister of
Police boasts about how uncorrupt and competen t our police force is, and she is largely
right about that, but how is it going to help to cut their salaries?
But today I do not want to talk about that so much as about the evidence last week
that we saw of National’s education policy to increase class sizes and to cut technology
learning in our intermediate schools crashing and burning. What a humiliating
backdown for Hekia Parata. What an embarrassment that was for her and the National
Government. I will give you this guarantee. There will not be a single National MP who
gets up and praises the National Governme nt’s Budget policy on education. You know,
the only thing I regret about the embarrassment that Hekia Parata faced was that the two
major architects of that polic y, John Key and Bill Englis h, were nowhere to be seen
when she had to front up and back down. They were nowhere to be seen.
Do not tell me, members of the National Government, that Bill English did not know
exactly what that Budget policy meant. It was in the briefing paper to him as Minister
last year—increase class sizes, it said. Then  the Secretary to the Treasury, Gabriel
2820 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
Makhlouf, gave a speech just 2 months ago sa ying that the way to improve quality in
education was to increase class sizes—in crease class sizes. Did National members
actually believe that? They pa rroted it for a fortnight. I bet we never hear it again from
them.
I was looking at a copy of the Listener the other day from 28 May 2005. There was
an interview with one Mr John Key. What was Mr Key saying? He was asked why he
sent his children to private sc hools. He said, really, it is “for educational reasons. Their
schools have smaller classes and are better resourced...”. That is what he said.

items.speaker: Hon Nanaia Mahuta
items.text: One rule.

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: One rule for Mr Key and for the majority of Cabinet who send
their kids to private schools, and another ru le for the rest of us, whose kids proudly go
to public education in this country. I want to  say that if it is good enough for kids in
private schools to have small classes so they  have more individual learning, then it is
good enough for all of our children. If we have a philosophy as New Zealanders, a set of
principles and ideology, it is the ideology of fairness. It says that some kids will come
from privileged and wealthy backgrounds—fin e. Other kids do not. But the really
important thing is that ever y child should get eq ual opportunity. Every child should be
able to achieve his or her potential. I will fight and fight and fight again against this
National Government, which says it will put mo re money into private education, but for
the kids who go to public schools it will incr ease their class sizes and close down their
technology classes.
You know, I do not exempt Ms Parata from th e blame of this policy altogether. She
has a job as Minister of E ducation—I once did that job—and  her job was to understand
the policy that was being proposed, to subject it to scrutiny, and to make a judgment as
to whether it was the right policy. [Interruption] I will ask Paul Goldsmith this question.
If she knew the impact on intermediate schools, why did she not tell her colleagues?

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: Is that a rhetorical question?

items.speaker: Hon PHIL GOFF
items.text: He has no answer—he has no an swer. If she knew and she did
not tell her colleagues, that was appallingl y bad judgment. And if she did not know the
consequences, that was simply incompetence and inadequacy on her part.
You know, we heard her going th rough the parroting of all of the explanations. Here
is a commentator in Saturday’s New Zealand Herald : she was “spouting meaningless
blather. Repeatedly mouthing platitudes …”. It is just not  good enough to parrot a line.
“The truth is”—and this is word for wor d—“that the Education Minister’s botched
handling of the cost-cutting blunder, which initially would have seen some schools
losing up to five teacher positions, has brutally exposed her political shortcomings.”
Under a Labour Government the educati on spokesperson is always on the front
bench, and to get on the front bench you have to  have political competence to be there.
But we have seen anything but political competence from this Minister. This policy was
a disgrace. It was a disgrace that she wa s hung out to dry by Bill English, who did not
front up alongside her, despite the fact that he knew what that policy meant, and it was
an equal disgrace from John Key to support a policy that was absolutely rejected by
parents right across our community. It is strange, I often th ink, how a number of people
in this House have benefited from the welfar e State in their time of  need, but when it
comes to extending the hand of help to kids who have need today, they do not want to
do it. They just want to cut; they want to make things worse.
John Key did say one thing that was interes ting, on Newstalk ZB. He said that he is
not arrogant enough not to listen to what people are saying. Well, I have got some
advice for Mr Key. In every public opinion poll th at has ever been held in this country,
people have said that they do not want to see New Zealand flogging off its public assets.
I wonder whether Mr Key is not  arrogant enough to ignore their views, because those
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2821
on the Finance and Expenditure Committee who have been going around the country
over the last month or two time and again h eard submissions from people utterly and
emphatically opposed to the sale of assets . Why would you sell the best-performing
assets that you have got? Thes e are the assets that Treasury it self admits are so efficient
that privatisation will not improve their e fficiency. Why would you sell the assets that
returned to us, 2 years ago, $700 million in  1 year, which, as John Key admitted, went
towards our hospitals and our schools? Why would you hand over ownership of
something that all of us as New Zealanders, as Kiwis, and as taxpayers own and benefit
from to only those who can afford to pa y for it? And why does the Government not
admit that most of those shares, the co rnerstone shareholding, will go into foreign
ownership? That is what Treasury says in its briefing to the Government.

items.speaker: This was a zero Budget
items.text: zero extra spen ding, zero contributi on to growth, zero
vision, and zero hope. The only thing that it will continue to do is to send New
Zealanders, the 1,000 a week who are leaving, out of this c ountry and into Australia.
One school in my electorate, which was men tioned in the paper this morning, Wesley
Intermediate School, has lost 14 percent of its roll in the last year to Australia. This
Government has failed, this Budget is a loser,  and we are seeing the last term of this
National Government.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: What we have heard there, from
the former leader of the Labour Party, is just so much negative claptr ap, is it not? It is
no wonder that that member was rejected by most New Zealanders at the 2011 election.
It is because he was so negative. Here we  have this Government, in the Budget of 2012,
in very tough economic times, that has de livered a very pragmatic Budget for these
economic times. When you look at the dark gr ey clouds gathering in Europe, and when
you think about what those members on the ot her side of the House would do if they
were sitting over here on the Treasury benc hes, we know what they would do. They
would spend more and increase taxes. Our debt would just blow  out and balloon, and
we would end up in a situation like many countries in Europe now. Some of the
countries over there have 50 percent unemp loyment. We see now Spain with a $100
billion bailout of its banks. These are the issues that New Zealand has to face. But over
on the other side you hear Phil Goff, the form er leader of the Labour Party, so negative.
Where is the aspiration? Where is the posit ive talk? There is not hing. There is nothing
from the Labour Opposition. Whereas under th e stewardship of the finance Minister,
Bill English, with the overwhelming support of our Prime Minister, we have delivered a
Budget that has been difficult to bring toge ther under these economic  times, but where
we have found new spending, reprioritised  spending, of about $4.4 billion or $4.5
billion, reinvested into core public services.
Most New Zealanders know that we have to  tighten our belts. Most New Zealanders
know that we have to rein in debt. Most New Zealanders  know that we have to lift
productivity and grow the economy. That is why it is great, under this Government, that
our economy has grown in nine out of the last 10 quarters. Is not th at fantastic? We are
growing. When you look at the countries that  we like to compare ourselves with, and
those that I have just talked  about in Europe where they are not growing, New Zealand
is growing. We are going to grow a lo t more jobs; about 150,000 are forecast by
Treasury in the next 4 years. In the last  couple of years the economy has grown 60,000
jobs.
Just in the last week we had Minist er Paula Bennett talkin g about unemployment
and how that dropped considerably down to  about 50,000 in May—fantastic—a drop of
more than 3,500 in the last month. What is also topical is the young people who are
getting back into employment. That peaked  in January 2010 at about 23,500; now it is
13,500. Is that not fantastic? You heard from the Prime Minister today that about 20,000
2822 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
people have moved off the unemployment bene fit in the last couple of years. The
economy is growing, and that is as a result of  the tough decisions that have been made
by this Government under the stewardship of the Minister of Finance, Bill English.
Think also about the vulnerable. Under tough economic times, we have supported
those whom we needed to support—for example, those on Working for Families, and
superannuitants. Superannuation is up by about 20 percent since 2008—fantastic. War
pensions are up. And we have a real fo cus on getting even more people off the
unemployment benefit and into work. Minist er Paula Bennett is doing a fantastic job
there. We need to support her.  We need to ensure that thes e New Zealanders are able to
perform in our modern-day economy. That is where it comes down to education. Yes,
we have had a robust discussion about educatio n. It has been interesting to hear all of
the issues that have been raised—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Your policy crashed and burned. Just admit it.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: —since the Budget was announced  in the last few weeks.
One of the things—

items.speaker: Hon Phil Goff
items.text: Two weeks and you had to withdraw it. That’s how bad it was.

items.speaker: Hon NATHAN GUY
items.text: —that the Opposition and Phil Go ff, who is chipping in now,
have not talked about in his negative rant is  why the performance of  our teachers is not
improving. Why have we still got one in five children failing in our education system?
Why has the tale of underachievement been constant under the Labour Government for
9 years? Now this Government is keen to addr ess that to ensure that we lift the tale of
underachievement. Why did we have our oppon ents so negative when we rolled out
national standards? Why did we have that? That was because they were supporting the
teacher unions. Now parents have plain reporting coming on to the kitchen table. They
know how well their children are doing, and they know where to put the support for
their children so that they can continue to lift the standards of numeracy and literacy.
What we have from the Opposition is no debate talking about why there has been a
13 percent increase in teacher roll growth ove r the last 10 years when the student roll
growth has been about 2.5 percent. Teacher roll growth is up here, student roll growth is
lower, yet the quality and the performance of our students coming out of our education
system have not improved. That is where the debate now needs to focus on, in my
opinion.
This has also been a great Budget for he alth—$435 million extra invested in health,
and there is a lot more going into resear ch and innovation, which is part of our
economic growth agenda. We are also puttin g more money into our assets, as well.
Think about what is happening in our Stat e highway network up and down the country.
Roads of national significance are going thro ugh the consenting process, which has
been fast-tracked under this Government, like Transmission Gully and the Waterview
Connection. All of these ones that would have probably take n about 5 years on average
under the previous Government have now  been put through an Environmental
Protection Authority process of about 9 months.
My constituents in the Ōtaki electorate are saying “B ring it on for Transmission
Gully, bring it on for the Kapiti Expressway, ensure that we can improve our safety
performance on our State highway network, lift  productivity, and continue to grow our
regional economic growth.” But what we ha ve from our opponents over there is such
negative claptrap. They over there on “Planet Labour” are not aspirational at all. They
have continued to worry about their leadersh ip woes. It was interesting when I had a
look at my Saturday Dominion Post. The interesting thing about the leadership woes in

items.speaker: Labour continues. Here we are
items.text: “The ma n waiting in the wings”, Grant Robertson.
There was a lovely story on Grant Robertson— just what, I am sure, David Shearer, the
new leader, would not want. Is it not amazi ng, when you have the battle of the three
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2823
Davids still ongoing, and here you have Gran t Robertson, the deputy of David Shearer,
having a blow-by-blow piece in C3 in the inside of the Saturday Dominion Post? What
was interesting in here was that “Mr Robert son lives by three rules:”. The first one you
might be interested to hear about is “treat  others how you want to be treated”. Well, I
would have thought it is ironic that Grant Robertson wants to treat David Shearer in this
way, with a full-blown article with a heading saying “The man waiting in the wings”.
The Labour leadership woes continue. Da vid Shearer continues to bumble, and
stumble, and stammer, and stutter his wa y through interview after interview. Grant
Robertson is loading the deckchairs up there in the office. He is getting his staff
appointed in. Mark my words, by the end of the year Grant Robertson will be the next
leader of the Labour Party.
Anyway, I will get back on to the issues about this very important Budget, which has
been carefully crafted by the Minister of  Finance and well received by most New
Zealanders. The thing that I am very passionate about as Minister of Veterans’ Affairs is
the 10 extra deployments that we announced in  this Budget. It was hard to find any new
money, but I put a pitch through Cabinet, and we managed to find $4.8 million for the
10 extra deployments. Those New Zealanders who have served in places like Rhodesia,
Afghanistan, Iraq, Iran, Cambodia, Somalia, Haiti, Bougainville, Sudan, and south
Lebanon will now be able to ge t a war disablement pension. It  is a fantastic initiative,
supported by this Government in tough economic  times. Most important, as I wrap up,
this is a Budget that has been well deliver ed, and well received by New Zealanders, and
thank goodness we have got a decent Prime Minister in John Key.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Speaker. It
is a pleasure to rise after the Hon Nathan G uy, as he finished on discussing the 10 extra
deployments and the war disablement pensions that he was able to deliver through this
Budget 2012.
As I start out, it is interesting to reflect on what has been happening around the globe
in just the week that has been. Spain has applied for a €100 billion bailout of its banking
system, which could see its public debt rise to over 90 percent of GDP. In that country
alone, Spain, nearly 50 percent of its youth—25-year-olds and under—are unemployed,
unable to find jobs, and without a future ahead  of them. So to be able to stand here
today in the context of what is happeni ng in Spain, Italy, Greece, Portugal—in fact,
Ireland and the UK as well—and debate this  Budget, which Bill English has put
forward, is a wonderful opportunity.
Let us put it in context in regard to those other countries. This Budget will keep
Crown debt below 30 percent of GDP—30 per cent. It is about 23 percent now, at its
maximum rising to 28 to 30 percent of GDP. That  is a wonderful posi tion to be in as a
country, particularly compared with those European nations. Our long-term objective by
2020 is to get that debt back down to 20 percent of GDP. We have set an objective of
getting back to surplus in the 2014-15 year, and I am confident that that will happen,
especially on the back of the fact that ju st last week Minister English announced that
this year’s Budget deficit is over $1 billion less than we had forecast. This was for two
key reasons—important reasons: firstly, in creased revenue of about $700 million, but
also, importantly, $300 million additional savi ngs over and above what we forecast.
That is a fantastic situation to be in.
On top of that, we see an announcement by Minister Paula Bennett saying that there
are 20,000 additional jobs, and that the unemployment be nefit numbers right now—
today, in the middle of very difficult times—a re the lowest they have been since 2009.
On any basis this is a great space to be in.
In thinking about this Budget, I am calling it the “hard yards Budget”. It is where this
Government is doing th e hard yards to get us through a nd back to surplus, back to a
2824 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
position where our debt is starting to come bac k. It is a bit like the forwards in a rugby
pack. This Budget is a props, hookers, and locks Budget, where they pick up the ball
from the back, take just an extra yard, and get closer to that finishing line. This is not a
wingers Budget or a full backs Budget.

items.speaker: Paul Goldsmith
items.text: No show ponies.

items.speaker: Hon CHRIS TREMAIN
items.text: This is not a show ponies Budget. This is a hard yards
Budget that will return this country back to surplus, bringing our debt down. I think that
is important.
Over and above all that, wh at we are seeing throughou t the public sector is a
revolution taking place. A quiet  revolution is occurring. I wa nt to thank public servants
around the country for the job that they are do ing to assist us in bringing this country
back into surplus. But that is happening not only in the Public Service but in NGOs
throughout the nation. In that regard, I wanted to focus on a couple of  initiatives in my
own electorate, back in Napier. One is ar ound the Napier Kindergarten Association and
an issue that came to the table a couple of Budgets ago. We introduced a policy that was
not popular at that point in time where we capped the spend on teachers to an 80 percent
level of qualified teachers at early childhood education centres. Rightly so, at the time
the industry was up in arms about that and was concerne d about that. I attended an
AGM where the association was very concer ned about that funding and what it would
do to it.
But today I want to talk a bout the association’s AGM th is year and what it has
actually done. A year on from that, despite all the dramas that were predicted and all the
issues that it thought might come into play, these are its profit and loss figures: in 2010
it was fortunate to make a $320,000 profit. Given all the concerns that were posed about
the drop in funding, one would have thought that things w ould get a little bit more
difficult. Well, the 2011 financial account s show a $339,000 profit.  So I want to
congratulate that association on the wonderful j ob that it has done in very difficult
times.
But here is the interesting point. This is how it achieved that result. I am going to
read from its financial manager’s report. It says: “It’s important to note that in taking on
and dealing with these issues, we are going to do a number of things. Strategies we
employed to minimise the impact of th e funding cuts included introducing Friday
afternoon sessions, being open for the maximu m number of days available to us,
diversifying a couple of the kindergartens to all-day licen ces, and”—here is the real
kicker—“being prudent with expenditure, renegotiating serv ice costs where possible.”
My goodness! Is that not terrible! These guys ar e to be congratulated because what they
have done is, given the difficult times we are in, they have risen to the mark and have
delivered. They have delivered the same, if not  better, services with less money. That is
something to be congratulated on, and I am proud that my kindergarten association has
risen to the plate in that regard and delivered these amazing savings.
Outside of that, I want to talk about th e ministries that I am proud to be now
associated with as Minister, and the efforts they are making in that evolutionary process
to deliver better services to the public and w ith less money. I start with tourism, where
Kevin Bowler at Tourism New Zealand, Liz MacPherson at the Mi nistry of Economic
Development, and their teams are doing a ma gnificent job. They have refocused the
strategy to continue to drive additional tourists to our nation, while the segments around
the world—as Europe backs off, China rise s, Asia rises. They are refocusing their
strategy, reinforcing the “100% Pure New Zealand” brand, which is superb. But,
importantly, here is what they have really done, which is exciting. They have raised an
additional $25 million from the private sector for partnership funding—$25 million.
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2825
They are using that money to support the promotion of New Zealand and to increase
tourism opportunities here in New Zealand. That is fantastic.
The Ministry of Civil Defence and Emergency Management is ably led by John
Hamilton, and he is doing a wonderful job there.  It has delivered a 6 percent efficiency
gain to the Government, and that will help us to drive this Budget—this hard yards
Budget that I was previously talking about. Bu t while doing that, the ministry is still
delivering superb services. It is focusing on lifting the capability of our 16 regions.
Through that, I just want to thank those regi ons that have had to deal with severe
weather events since I have been the Minister of Civil Defence, particularly Nelson,
Taranaki, and Northland.
My larger ministry, which is the Departme nt of Internal Affairs, is a wonderful
ministry. It really is the hear t and soul of New Zealand. It deals with citizenship on the
one side through to censorship on the other. And those guys in the censorship
compliance unit, as I said when I stood and took a question in the House recently, did a
wonderful job in bringing those 55 people to  task and saving those 12 children. These
guys work in a tough environment and are doing a great job.
One of the wonderful opportunities we have in  the Department of Internal Affairs is
to deliver on result area No. 10. It is one of the 10 results that the Prime Minister has put
his hand on the table and said that we will be held accountable for doing these things,
such as lifting the level of early childhood education to 98 per cent of children and
getting National Certificate of Educatio nal Achievement pass rates from around 68
percent, where they are now, to 85 percent. But result area No. 10 is where I have some
responsibility. That is about giving New Z ealanders the opportunity to have a much
stronger digital interf ace with the Government, and maki ng it easier for them to work
with the Government in a digital environmen t. We have a range of projects that I am
proud to see the department delivering on in that regard, allowing citizens to have a
stronger relationship with the Government. There are a couple th at I have announced
just recently that will see huge savings. Last  week alone we confirmed an IBM contract
that will see significant savings in the order of $250 million over a 10-year period.
There are huge savings with the one.govt network, which will see $400 million to $600
million in savings. I mean, this is real mone y that we can deliver back into education
and health and deliver more surgical operations and better education for our kids.
I am proud of what is happe ning with this Budget. We are driving revolutionary
change, and this is an exciting time for New Zealanders. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: On 5 June the Prime
Minister sent out a letter to residents in th e Christchurch East electorate. It was done
electorate by electorate, whether or not  the Government had a constituency MP
2826 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
representing that electorate. John Key sent it out in his name, and he said that the
rebuild of Greater Christchurch was central to the plan that  was set out in Budget 2012.
The Government’s narrative ar ound the earthquake recovery in  Christchurch or greater
Christchurch as it refers to it—because, of course, Waimakarir i District Council and
Selwyn District Council are in cluded within the greater Christchurch area—was very
clear. The Government is putting a lot of mo ney into the rebuild of Christchurch, and
that means that it does not have money avai lable for other things that have suddenly
become the “nice-to-haves”. The people of Ch ristchurch are actually sick and tired of
this Government using them as an excuse to  sell our country’s assets and to do things
like put extra taxes on our newspaper delivery kids. The newspaper deliver kids in
Christchurch have had a pretty hard job of  it getting through the streets after all the
earthquake damage, and finding their pockets be ing picked by the Government to make
up the nickels and dimes in this sort of Budget is absolutely unreasonable.
But for the Government to talk about what is happening in Christchurch as an excuse
for what it is doing to the rest of the country is in tolerable, given what we have already
experienced in Christchurch. It  is about time that we were allowed to speak the truth in
this House about what has really been going on, as the Gove rnment has entirely
politicised the situation in Christchurch to its own advantage—even from the moment
that it chose the corporate colours for th e Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority.
What colours do you think most people in  New Zealand would associate with
Canterbury? It would be red and black, woul d it not? You would expect the corporate
colours of the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery  Authority to be red and black. Actually
they were going to be red and black. The Mi nister had a special jacket made—red and
black with the label CERA on the front of it—very shortly after the February
earthquake. After the Canterbury Earthquake  Recovery Authority had been set up he
had that red and black jacket on. But guess which corporate colour  it settled on? It
settled on blue. What association does blue  have with Christc hurch? None—absolutely
none. So it was a subliminal message. There are those who say colours do not matter,
but actually, in Christchurch, colours do matte r, because if your pr operty is red zoned,
or green zoned—now with a blue tinge over th e top of it—then it certainly does matter.
It matters to your equity. It matters to your future. It matters to any decisions that you
can make. It matters to your relationship with your insurance company. There is nothing
that matters more in Christchurch at the moment than colours. National started the
colour regime with its own decision to put  the National Party brand on the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Authority. The sub liminal message is that the National
Government is rebuilding Christchurch. Cant erbury cannot even own its own recovery
with its own colours leading the way, red and black.
That is something that Labour would restate straight away, and th at is that red and
black would be leading the recovery. We woul d let the people of Canterbury own their
own recovery. We would not have a to p-down Government department and a
Government Minister actually controlling the recovery of our city and making all of
these decisions without any engagement w ith the people. We would put a layer of
governance between the Minister  and Roger Sutton, who is th e head of the Canterbury
Earthquake Recovery Authority, which would become a State-owned enterprise or an
independent Crown entity, in order for it to be able to do its job properly, which is to
facilitate the recovery. It is something that  has got to be owned by the people, with a
proper sense of engagement with the people, so that they can be involved in it.
Let us have a look at what the Government is saying in its narrative. It has set aside
$5.5 billion for the Canterbury Earthquake R ecovery Fund and then goes on to say that
more than $3.4 billion of the recovery fund will have been spent by next year. Well, that
is not true. We know that that  is not true, because, in fact, we have done the sums. The
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2827
Government has thrown everything into the $5.5 billion that it can  possibly find. It has
got $4 million to establish the Canterbury Earthquake Recovery Authority, $3 million
for the royal commission of inquiry, $23 millio n for work that was already done before
the 22 February earthquake even happe ned, a $5 million donation to the Red Cross
Society Inc., $20 million on the national controller and civil defence costs, and $100
million for the AMI contingency, which originally was $300 million - odd.
Then it has added in what it would have to pay for its own asset repairs—schools and
State highways. That is in there. It is over $80 million so far and increasing. Of course
there is the total amount allocated to repa iring local infrastruc ture—$1.6 billion over 5
years—which represents the 60 percent of the cost the Crown is already liable for under
the pre-existing arrangements between central  government and local government in the
case of a natural disaster.
When we analyse the Budget numbers we di scover that the Gove rnment had shifted
just over $1 billion from the forecasts allo cated in the pre-electi on fiscal update to the
yet-to-be-allocated category and then claimed that as part  of the $2.17 billion projected
spend this year. I am afraid that is just  smoke and mirrors, and that is what the
Government has been doing with this. The reality is that the Government has really
played tricks with people’s confidence over a serious disast er and I think it should be
held to account for doing that.
Of course in this letter it goes on to repeat  all of these other things over and over
again. The Government has “repaired over 15,500 homes”. Well, it has not paid for that.
That is being paid for by either the Eart hquake Commission or th e insurance industry,
so that is not something that the Govern ment has had to pay for. Twelve thousand
square metres of road have been repaired. Well, actually that is included in the sum it
has already mentioned, and also the additional amount on installing drinking-water pipe,
waste-water pipe, and demolishing 80 percent of unsafe buildings. Those things are all
paid for out of other budgets, and so it is ju st restating it. The Government has purchase
offers to more than 6000 residential red z one homeowners, and two-thirds have been
accepted, but it does not say that the underlyi ng assumption was that 100 percent would
accept option one. Actually, 25 percent of thos e who have accepted one of the options
have accepted option one. So its assumptions are completely wrong and it has not done
the numbers again. It is not telling people the truth. It is not being up front with people,
and this should be the most open and tran sparent process. There should be open
engagement with the people.
It is fast tracking planning permission to make thousands of new residential sections
available in new subdivisions on safe land. We ll, when do they come? Too late for the
people who have to move out of the red zone . Not one single one of those sections will
be available to rebuild on by April next year—not one of t hose that they have fast
tracked the planning permission for. Then it is completing the infrastructure repairs and
undertaking a further amount each month on aver age. Again, that is restating the figure
it has already included in the original figures. But then what does it do? It says that you
can have your say now. It is time for you to have your say, and let us just restate our
position on this. The letter says: “Pease tick the three aspects of the Government’s
commitment to rebuilding greater Christchurch  that are most important to you:”. So, of
course, it is reinforcing to the public that the Government  has got this commitment to
rebuilding greater Christchurc h, and that is because the Na tional Government is doing
it. It is not facilitating people to do it for themselves.

items.speaker: But then it goes on to say this
items.text: “Please tick one of the following options: I ALWAYS
support the following political party: Unite d Future, Green, Maori, Labour, National,
Act, NZ First. OR I USUALLY support the following political party:”, and it has set out
the political parties again. Th en it says “OR I don’t supp ort any political party in
2828 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
particular.” Then it says: “Privacy notice.  Supplying this information is voluntary. The
information is being collected by National MPs in their capacity as Members of
Parliament to be used for electorate and related activity.” Well, this letter is for Wigram.
The other one that I have got here is for Christchurch East. I am  afraid that Megan
Woods is the MP for Wigram, and I am the MP for Christchurch East, but it suggests
that people go to “Our Christchurch Cent ral MP Nicky Wagner”, who is “available to
assist you with constituency issues”. Nicky Wagner will not help her own constituents
with these issues and, in fact, we have had to take up the wo rk that she has left behind.
So what—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: The taxpayer paid for that.

items.speaker: Hon LIANNE DALZIEL
items.text: And the taxpayer has paid for this to go out there to find
out how people are voting, and to actually fi nally come clean and show that National
has been entirely political about this from st art to finish. It has not worked with the
people about the issues that really matter. Wh at I am concerned about is that we have
got people who now live in different parts of  electorates who have to put up with this
over and over again. This photograph is of re d zone land; this photograph is of green-
blue land. It is not fair that the Governme nt will not work with the people in order to
ensure that they understand what is going on.
I would like to seek leave of the House to table an example of the correspondence
that the Rt Hon John Key has put into my electorate of Christchurch East.
