items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: There was a speech that focused on the
burning issues of the day, did it not—the  colours of the Canterbury Earthquake
Recovery Authority! Goodness me! In this debate  I just want to talk about the issue of
fiscal policy in general and the fairness of our tax system. I find myself in the unusual
position of reflecting back on Budget 2010, and the reason for that is the many
references made in this House to the cost  of tax cuts for thos e in the upper income
bracket—in particular, the references from  Dr Norman, who has gone on ad nauseam
over the last month about his belief that the National Government’s tax cuts in 2010, far
from being fiscally neutral, actually cost “$2 billion and counting”. I have got no ability
to say whether or not that figure is correct, but whether or not it is, it is certainly not the
full story. In fact, it seems that Dr Norm an may have been taking some policy advice
from the former member Stuart Nash. Reme mber Mr Nash in this House last year
talking about farming incomes?

items.speaker: Hon Amy Adams
items.text: That’s right.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: That is right—remember ? He talked about gross
incomes. Never mind that that is not wh at one pays tax on. One pays tax on net
incomes. Well, Dr Norman is telling half the story really, really well, because whether
or not the cost of the tax cuts to the upper income earners was $2 billion, that was just
one element of about 13 or more separate leve rs to fiscal policy that this Government
has made, including increases to GST that have resulted in upper income earners paying
much, much more of that tax, the removal of depreciation on residential and commercial
rentals, and the closure of a number of loopholes that were unintended consequences
that benefited upper income earners in tax transfers like Working for Families, student
allowances, and child support. Those loopholes were actually introduced by Labour and
supported by the Greens. But the biggest on e—the biggest one of all—was that the
difference between the trust top tax rate and the top personal rates was so wide. I
remember the Tax Working Group actually said th at in the past we had one of the least
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2829
distortionary tax systems in the OECD, and then  we went from that to one of the most
distortionary under Labour.
So although there was a reduction in the top personal tax rate in 2012 to remove that
distortion, it is completely incorrect to say that that had a cost of $2 billion. I much
prefer to refer to the more independe nt and non-partisan commentaries of the
accounting firm of Deloitte, which in its 2011 Budget report confirmed that the 2010 tax
switch was “indeed fiscally neutral accordin g to the tax bands”. As far as I am
concerned, that argument was over more than a year ago. Dr Norman can go on and on
and on all he likes, but that does not make it any more true. Indeed, those changes that
we made meant that three-qua rters of New Zealanders pay a top personal marginal tax
rate of 17.5 percent. Half of  all households pay no net tax at all, and 17 percent—17
percent—of households pay 97 percent of the net income tax burden in this country.
But Labour and the Greens say 97 percen t is not enough. They would want to put
that top tax rate back up and punish hard -working New Zealanders even more. We
know what they would do with those tax increases. The cuts actually gave New
Zealanders a choice, and those cuts came acros s the board. They had a choice to either
spend them, save them, or reduce debt with  them. We now know what they did with
them. They saved them and they reduced debt  with them, because our savings rate is
going up and our private debt is going down. But Labour and the Greens do not think
that the public should have a right to deci de what to do with their money. They think
they know better than the public how the public should spend their money. So they went
to the electorate last year and they said: “We are going to take those cuts back off you.
We are going to take that tax cut back off you, because we know better how to spend
it.” Well, I think the electorate spoke very clearly about what it thought about that
policy. It spoke then and it spoke now—

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: You’re making it up!

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: I would like to know what that member thinks I am
making up, because absolutely every one of th ese things has been verified. The people
around him are not making any noises about it, because they know what the truth of it
is. They know what the positive impact of t hose tax cuts and fiscal prudence was. And
that is what the electorate knew too, becau se this Government  does not treat the
electorate like idiots. We can go to the electorate with tough decisions like partial floats,
like the mixed-ownership model—

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: Like class sizes.

items.speaker: MICHAEL WOODHOUSE
items.text: —yes, like class sizes—that is right. And, OK, maybe
there is another discussion still to be had, but  at least we are listening. At least we are
listening, and that is a damn sight more than  the public is doing to the policies of those
members. Who knows what those policies ar e? There is no alternative being thrown up
except tax, borrow, and spend. I think the public has spoken very clearly about that.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: One of the things New Zealanders hold very
dear is feeling safe in their homes. It is one of those things that my constituents hold
very dear. In fact, I know a number of people move to th e South Island and to small
towns in the South Island becau se that is where they feel  safe. They feel safe going
about their business, th ey feel safe on the roads, and th ey feel safe in their homes, and
that is something that I believe we will want for all New Zealanders all throughout New
Zealand.
That is why National embarked, when it came into Government, on a comprehensive
programme of reform to protect our comm unities: to protect everybody in New Zealand
on the roads, at work, a nd in their homes, to prev ent crime happening to New
Zealanders, and to put victims at the heart of the justice system. In the time that the
National Government has been in power we have passed 80 new laws to do with the
2830 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
safety of New Zealanders. We have introdu ced pieces of legislation like the offender
levy, where $50 is taken from offenders and put towards the victim s of crime. I was
looking for the latest figure of how much has been gained from the offender levy, and I
am afraid I cannot find it. It is not to hand, but I know that it is a significant amount and
I know that that offender levy is making a real difference to the victims of crime in New
Zealand.
This Government has given victims more say in court with victim impact statements.
This Government has put 600 more police on the beat—on the front  line—in the small
towns and the cities throughout New Zealand. This Government has provided tools to
seize the proceeds of crime. Again, the amount recovered from the proceeds of crime is
indeed significant and that money is, in tu rn, being put to good use. This Government
has brought in tougher sentenci ng and parole laws and now is  looking at bail laws for
all New Zealanders. We have tackled gangs, we have tackled P, and we are making
significant gains on th e importation of precursors of P.  This Government has also
worked on road safety and we now have the lowest road toll in 50 years.
But, of course, that is not enough. B udget 2012 has a strong focus once again—and I
am very pleased to see it—on law and order. Recorded crime is now  at a 15-year low,
and the crime rate, which is set at a rate per 100,000 of population, is at a 30-year low.
Those are figures that are to be celebrated, but, according to  the Minister of Police and
Minister of Corrections, Anne Tolley, much  more needs to be done. What a great
attitude from our Minister of  Police and Minister of Correct ions. This is a Minister and
a Government committed to making our co mmunities safer, with a focus now on
prevention—that is, preventing crime from happening and also reducing crime.
Budget 2012 supports this target for safer communities for New Zealanders. It
supports this target and builds on the achievement of less crime. This Budget
reprioritises $65 million in operating expendi ture over the next 4 years and this
expenditure is targeted in certain direc tions. There will be 33,000 offenders, including
remand prisoners, accessing drug and alcohol treatment.
This Government has already banned smoking in our prisons. It was probably about
1½ years ago that smoking was banned in ou r prisons—a move that has been reported
to us in the Law and Order Committee as an  outstanding success. There is cleaner air
both for officers and for inmates alike, im proved health—of course—as a consequence
of no smoke in the air, and a decrease in standover tactics now that tobacco has been
removed as a currency. I will never forget the day when the Department of Corrections
came to the Law and Order Committee and sh owed us a video and photographs of fires
in prisons. Prisoners wad up their bedding, sheets,  or paper, light it with their cigarette
lighters, throw it out into the corridor, a nd watch the ensuing mayhem, placing not only
corrections officers themselves but other pris oners at risk as the corrections officers
scramble to put out those fires. The incidence of fires is now virtually nil, and so it
would be fair to say that prisons are now a safer place for officers and inmates alike.
The Corrections Amendment Bill has passed its first reading. This is a bill that will
remove red tape, allowing our prisons to operate more effectively, and also, importantly,
that makes improvements to both drug testing and strip-searching procedures. All these
are measures to make our prison environments  safer for all those who have to live and
work in them.
Budget 2012 provides for more rehabil itation places. Again, the Law and Order
Committee is to travel to Rimutaka Prison this  week to have a look at this, and I extend
a welcome to any other members of Parliament  who would like to co me. It is a select
committee trip, but it is open to any other me mbers who are interested in law and order
issues and who would like to ta ke part in this visit. This visit will have a look at
rehabilitation programmes at work. These programmes are designed to equip prisoners
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2831
with the skills to face the world outside pr ison when they get released. As part of
Budget 2012 there will be 2,950 more prisoners  in education and training. There has
already been a 45 percent increase in New Zealand Qualifications Authority credits
gained by prisoners in trades training and wo rk skills. It is pretty obvious, is it not? The
more work skills a prisoner has and the more trades training skills  a prisoner has, the
greater the likelihood of getting employment on release; it is much enhanced. So, too, is
there less likelihood of prisone rs reoffending and ending right  back where they began:
in prison. It is notable, particularly follo wing the contribution by the member who was
so fixated on the colour red in a previous contribution, that in Christchurch there are
130 new places for trades training. Of course, those are skills that are going to be sorely
needed in the future in Christchurch, and those skills are around building, carpentry, and
those practical skills that are going to be sorely needed.
Corrections has looked very carefully at the way it operates, as part of an expenditure
review, and has identified the best investme nts with a view to reducing reoffending. By
seriously addressing these contributors of crime—things like drug and alcohol addiction
and lack of literacy and numeracy skills—we can reduce the likelihood of reoffending.
Budget 2012 supports the police in working smarter and better. Of course, by
working more efficiently, the police are pr oviding a better public se rvice to taxpayers,
which is a very strong focus of this Government, and they have a real impact on crime
rates in New Zealand. Police Minister A nne Tolley announced the Prevention First
strategy late last year, which outlines how police aim to prevent crime before it happens.
Most important, it puts the victim first, ulti mately making New Zealand a safer place to
work and to live. The strategy also aims to reduce the number of crashes on our roads,
to give police greater control of the criminal environm ent, to put the police on top, and
to provide a better service, once again, to victims. The Prevention First strategy puts
prevention of crime at the forefront of polic e security. It allows police to be more
proactive and work in a planned way. I was in terested to hear a policeman say to me
that gone are the days when the police car l eaves the police station, tosses a coin, and
then decides whether to turn left or right . Those days are gone. Now police are working
more effectively and smarter.
Budget 2012 supports front-line police with the provision of new technologies,
which gives them faster access to informati on so that they can make better decisions
when they are out on the road and facing crime. As the Prevention First and Policing
Excellence programmes continue to be rolled out, police are on course to reach the
target of a 13 percent reduction in crim e by 2014-15. That is a big goal. This Budget
supports that.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It is a pleasure to speak on the Appropriation Bill
and the 2012 Budget. Whatever this Budget is a future for,  it is not a Budget for the
future of New Zealand. It is miserly, it is penny-pinching, and it offers nothing for
future wealth creation and future wealth building for New Zealand. What we have seen
in this Budget—the headline issues for this Budget—is a tax on paper boys, we have
seen shifting the goalposts for elderly in th eir retirement and the support they get for
their retirement homes, we have seen more cu ts in front-line services, and we have seen
a lot of rhetoric accompanying the Budget, sa ying how wonderful it is for the future of
New Zealand. It is all Alice-in-Wonderland stuff. It is head-in-the-sand stuff. It is out of
touch. But the education changes that were  announced in this B udget—or, rather, not
announced, but presumed and implied—are something else again.
Let us recount what happened in relation to those education ch anges. The Treasury
Secretary was deployed for the softening-up pr ocess. So he gave the interview and he
gave the speech that signalled that class si ze was not the issue and that there would be
changes in the Budget and changes in financing for education. Nobody knew what was
2832 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
happening. No signal was given about the precise changes. What has become quite
apparent since the delivery of the Budget is that if Cabinet Minist ers knew, or even if
some of them knew, none of them asked the question and none of them reminded, or
told, their colleagues about what the imp act was going to be on the schools in their
electorates and the schools around the country. No one asked the question.
The sector itself did not know until the day before, or even the day of, the Budget. I
met intermediate school principals who did not know what the impact was going to be
until the morning of the Budget. That is how closely guarded this secret was. So the
education changes in the Budget were much  less Alice in Wonderland and much more
“malice in blunderland”. That is what that was about.
Budget 2012 offers nothing for the future of  New Zealand. Where in the Budget is
the foundation for future wealth creation? Wher e is the acceptance of the real and very
serious and difficult problems facing New Zealand on, for example, superannuation
financing and funding? What we do have from this Government and its economic and
finance policy is partially selling State-ow ned enterprises—the State assets—a policy
that we know is short-changing New Zeala nd in the long term. Even Treasury, in its
more honest moments, tells us that the yiel d, in terms of a sale price for those State
assets, will not make up for the return that  the Government gets on those in the longer
term. And we are not selling just State a ssets; now we are down to selling policy. So
when it comes to gambling and when it co mes to a convention centre in Auckland, we
will fund that through selling policy.
If ever there was a matter that was a case of “malice in blunderland”, surely it must
be ACC. I want to take a few moments to talk about the ACC issue, because this is
serious. ACC is a very important institution in this country. It is 38 years old this year.
It has been fundamental to  good health and safety a nd to good rehabilitation and
recovery for injured workers and for injured pe ople, and it is very important. It has long
held a high degree of public trust and c onfidence. Its genesis was in a bipartisan
decision of this Parliament to say that something had to change to provide for those who
are injured by accident.
It is unbelievable that many members opposite, in their speeches on the Budget so far
in this debate, have referred to the wonderful ACC reforms engendered by this
Government. So I want to talk about some  of those ACC reform s, because what we
have now is this important New Zealand inst itution with its reputation in tatters, all
because of the approach this Government has taken in relation to ACC.
The rot started under the previous Minister. One of the biggest political cons of a
generation was when this Government announced and declared and persuaded
everybody that ACC was in financial crisis. Never mind that for nearly 10 years ACC
had been generating surpluses of $1 billion. Ne ver mind that at that time it had reserves
of nearly $11 billion. The Government announced  that there was a fi nancial crisis, so it
got rid of many board members and installe d its specially recruited chairman, John
Judge, who now is no longer on the ACC board, at least. It recruited John Judge. It
hiked up the levies, totally unne cessarily, and when it got a backlash from the bikies,
whose bikes it could not crush, it had to backtrack at least on that part of it.
It hiked up the levies, and what has the imp act of that been? What has the impact of
that been? Well, up to about 2008-09, ACC gene rated surpluses of about $1 billion. It
used to spend about $2.5 billion to $3 bi llion on looking after people, on paying for
their medical treatment and medical costs, and on paying their compensation. Well, do
you know what happened last year? What happe ned last year was that ACC produced a
surplus of $3.5 billion. And do you know what  it spent on looking after people? Do you
know what it spent on the medical treatment a nd the care of people, and compensation?
It spent $2.9 billion. It generated a surplus greater than what it spent on every claimant
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2833
who needed medical care and treatment and who needed earnings-related compensation.
That is what it did.
The National Government was so embarrassed a bout it that just before the election,
lo and behold, it announced a reduction in the levies. That is how embarrassed it was
about its big mistake. But the mistake did not stop there.

items.speaker: Michael Woodhouse
items.text: Just apologise.

items.speaker: ANDREW LITTLE
items.text: It will never apologise about it. It will never apologise about
it, because this is a Government that, according to its own operations manual, does no
wrong—it does no wrong, apart from Nick Smit h. Nick Smith did admit that he did
wrong, and he did the honourable thing and stood down, but no other Minister has done
the same thing.
That was not the end of National’s ACC reforms. It put John Judge in for a reason. It
wanted to shake up the corporation. It wanted  to get into a programme of cost-cutting,
penny-pinching, and miserliness, and it want ed to push back on legitimate claimants—
people who had been injured through no fault of their own. It pushed back. One of those
people happened to be one of its own—Br onwyn Pullar, aided and abetted by another
one of its own, Michelle Boag. Of course , hell hath no fury like a scorned ACC
claimant who is a member of the National Party. And that is what happened.
So what we had were the ACC reforms promoted by this Government to get rid of a
good board and a good chair, hike up the le vies unnecessarily, de clare there is a
financial crisis, get into a dreadful progr amme of penny-pinching and cost-cutting, and
push back on legitimate claimants who are su ffering, who are in pain, and who are just
doing what every New Zealander has done for the last 38 years,  and that is to look to
ACC for help and support. The Government ha s created a culture of disentitlement, and
then cut back on those things that are needed to manage claimants’ personal information
needs carefully. Now we have an organisatio n whose reputation is in tatters, where
privacy breaches are endemic, and wh ere people are getting knocked back. These
people are suffering, exasperated, distressed, and depressed because of what this
Government’s ACC reforms have done.
The question is where the Minister is on th is. Where is the Minister on this? What
has she done? In the House today, when aske d what she had done and what her actions
were, she told us what everybody else had done. But what has she done?
Her challenge now is, having got rid of John Judge, to issue a new set of instructions.
Forget what the last Minister said, forget what Nick Smith said, and issue a new set of
instructions. Unfortunately, she has to issue them to Paula Rebstock, so we do not know
how much change there is going to be for this.

items.speaker: But here is the challenge to the Minister
items.text: issue a new set of instructions. Tell your
new board chair that we want an ACC that cares about the people who come to it for
help and support. Look after those people,  examine the claims, but look after those
people, and make sure that nobody who is en titled to support and assistance from ACC
is disentitled, rejected, denied, thrown out into the cold, and left to battle the behemoth
of ACC on their own, as so many are at the moment. Issue a new instruction. Say we
want a culture change, and make a difference, because never has a very important public
institution in New Zealand, which is so important to the life of New Zealand and the life
of New Zealanders, come under su ch sustained attack from th e people to whom it is so
important. Never has a public institution come under such sustained neglect from the
Minister who is responsible for it.
So that is the challenge. I look forward to this Government doing something new and
good for ACC, because that will be a change from the past 3½ years.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: I am very proud to stand and take a call in
this Budget 2012 debate. Over the last coupl e of weeks since Budge t day I have been
2834 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
taking the Budget to the people of the Taup ō electorate, which I am enormously proud
to represent. I have had post-Budget coffee catch-ups in places like Tirau, P ūtāruru,
Tokoroa, Cambridge, Taup ō, and T ūrangi. One of the things that has been quite
interesting is that I have been surprised at the fact that there have not actually been
many people who have been turning up with lo ts of questions to ask. I firmly believe
that that is because they know that this is a Budget for our times. This is a Budget that is
sensible, that is moderate, that is balanced, and that perfectly fits the times we are in. It
sets the path back to surplus, but, more important, it has that balance right in terms of
protecting those who need protection, and also  making sure that we have an economy
that is heading in the right  direction and that is grow ing, albeit slowly—slowly and
steadily. That is why I am proud of this Budget.
One of the things that has been really important is to remind the people of my
community about the broader context in which this Budget was delivered. I am
staggered that some on the other side of the House tend to forget some of the major
economic issues that this Government has faced. It came in after 9 years of Labour to
not only a recession already under way, a global financial crisis, a continuing
environment where there is still uncertainty in Europe, and a space that is changing by
the day but also the destruc tive earthquakes in Canterbury , which have come with a
price tag to the Crown of $20 billion. That side of the House tends to forget that that is
the context in which this Budget has been set.
The reality is that although we would like to have really certain times in front of us,
they are not, and they are not going to be fo r quite some time. So this is a Budget that
has taken that into consider ation. But we have still mana ged to put new spending into
the areas that matter—new spending into  areas like science and innovation, new
spending into health, new spending into education, and new spe nding into reducing
areas, like my colleague Jacqui Dean spoke ab out before, in terms of getting on top of
crime. These are the things that people in my electorate say are important. So this
Government is spending the money exactly where New Zealanders want it to be spent.
We are managing the finances tightly, we ar e building a more competitive environment,
we are making sure that the recipe is in  place for businesses to grow, and we are
rebuilding Canterbury, getting that city and that region back on its feet, all the while
with international challenges still in front of us.
It is really interesting because what we  are spending in Budget 2012 is exactly what
New Zealanders are asking for—exactly what New Zealanders are asking for. However,
we are spending through savings. That should be no surprise to anyone in this House, if
they are in direct contact with the people th ey represent, because that is exactly what
individuals, families, businesses, and community organisations are doing up and down
this country. They do not have new wads of  money that float th rough their doors on a
daily basis. They are making do with what th ey have, and that is exactly what this
Government is demonstrating. It is not a “slash-and-burn Budget”; it is a responsible
Budget. We have a very tight  constraint on the spending we have, and we are spending
new spending on the areas that count to New Zealanders.
If we look at health, for example, there is  $1.5 billion going in to health. Where is
some of that spending going? Well, it is go ing into things like faster treatment for
people who have cancer. If a nyone in this House has dea lt with or spent time with
someone in that situation, they  know that that is important to ordinary New Zealanders.
So that is the priority on this side of the House, and that is exactly what we are doing.
In terms of welfare reform, the approach th at this Government is  taking is saying:
“Well, actually, we might have to spend a bit more money up front.” Spending the
money up front to get families and individu als out of poverty and out of the welfare
benefit trap is worth it. That is anothe r area that New Zealanders up and down this
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2835
country are saying they are supportive of. They support exactly what this Government is
doing. New Zealanders are supporting exactly what we are doing.
Let us talk education.

items.speaker: Andrew Little
items.text: Yeah, yeah, quick.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Yes, absolutely. I am very pleased to talk about education. I am
very proud to be part of this side of the H ouse and to be part of a party that has an
unrelenting focus on lifting student achie vement—unrelenting, unrelenting. Do you
want me to say it again? Student achieve ment is the focus of this Government—
absolutely. In this one—

items.speaker: Phil Twyford
items.text: How about those class sizes, then?

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Yes, absolutely. I am more than happy to talk about the class
sizes. What happened was that parents told us that they were concerned about where
that might go. So what did we do? What did we do? We responded exactly to the
feedback that we were given. And do you know  what I have had si nce then? I have had
texts, I have had emails, and I have had phone calls fr om people saying: “Thank you.
Thank you for listening.” Do you know why memb ers on that side of the House are so
plugged in about it? It is becau se they never listened. They never listened. They never
responded. They are so out of touch with or dinary New Zealanders. They cannot handle
the fact that we are willing to say: “ OK, let’s say we are focusing on student
achievement.” That side of the House clearly did not do it, because it left one in five
children behind, and we are not willing to do that. We are not willing to leave one in
five of our young people behind. That is clearly demonstrated in some of the results and
some of the targets that we have set in our public services. Members opposite are going
quiet.
In early childhood education, 98 percent partic ipation is what we have set for our
young people. If you ask any primary school teacher who teaches a new entrant class
what makes the difference in terms of them t eaching those children, the answer is that it
is early childhood education—absolutely. And we have been spending more money
than Labour ever spent in 9 years in Government.

items.speaker: Hon Maryan Street
items.text: Quite wrong.

items.speaker: LOUISE UPSTON
items.text: Spending absolutely has increase d, and that side of the House
just cannot handle it. What else have we set in terms of targets? The next one—and I am
happy to say that it is ambitious—is to have 85 percent of our school leavers leave with
National Certificate of Educational Achiev ement level 2 by 2016. That is going to be
tough. That is going to be a challenge. But doe s this side of the House shy away from a
challenge like that? Absolutely not, because it  is worth it. This side of the House is
focused on results.
One of the results that my colleague Jacqui  Dean talked about in the area of law and
order, which is another area that is particularly important to the people of the Taup ō
electorate, is keeping our families and our communities safer. If you look at the target
that we have set in terms of reducing pr isoner reoffending, if we reduce that by 25
percent, that translates to 18,500 fewer victims ever y year—18,500 fewer victims. That
is the sort of thing that th is side of the House is fo cused on, and that is why New
Zealanders are supporting what we are doing. They trust that our Budget, our plan, will
get the results that they are interested in.
I am proud of Budget 2012. I am proud of what  we have delivered, despite being in
tough times. I recognise, listening to my constituents on a daily basis, that individuals,
families, businesses, and communities have been doing it tough. I recognise that, and I
hear it nearly daily. But this side of the House, unlike thos e who live on “Planet
Labour”, does not want to wish away the re cession. We are not pretending that there is
no global financial crisis. We are not prete nding that Canterbury does not come with a
2836 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
$20 billion price tag. We are actually taking the actions, slowly, surely, moderately,
sensibly, and deliberately, which will get New Zealand where we all want it to be.
Things are getting better. Our economy is growing slowly and surely. The number of
jobs is growing—17,000 in Christchurch alon e. Business confidence is growing. Our
major export markets of Asia and Australia are growing—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Your time has expired.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is an honour and
privilege to talk to this B udget 2012 debate. The context in which we assess this debate
is to look back at 3½ years of this Governme nt, and what did we inherit? We inherited
an economy that had some of the highest in terest rates in the world—over 10 percent.
Labour’s grave legacy was 5 consecutive years of contracting exports. Treasury
forecasts were particularly grim, with predic tions of deficits that  would go out over 10
years.
The prolonged global economic recession, the Christchurch earthquake, and
Labour’s economic mismanagement have led to a long, dark night in our history.
However, after a long, dark night, this Budget represents morning again in New
Zealand. It is morning again in New Zeal and because this Budget will balance the
Government’s books by the year 2015. It is morning again in New Zealand because this
Budget delivers better Government services. It is morning again in New Zealand as this
Budget builds a more productive and competitive economy.
Under this National Government, the economy has steadily built up to the point
where this morning 2,230,000 New Zealanders went to work—more than at any time in
our history. Interest rates are at historic lows, under 5 perc ent today, whereas they were
over 10 percent in 2008. Finally, inflation was over 5 percent in mid-2008, and it is now
at a low of 2.1 percent.
The Opposition has asked in this debate why it is important to balance the books.
Well, it is important because as we look ar ound the world, there are danger signs of
countries where out-of-control debt has brought nations to their knees. In Greece, where
crazy debt levels have led to a €130 billion rescue pack age for an economy that is
only—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I apologise. I know that
we are having problems with our speaker system and getting people’s voices out
uninterrupted to the world, but I think there has been an overcompensation. If you could
ask—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: This is not a point of order.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: If you could ask for the system to be turned down a little in
the House. I am a member who is slightly  hard of hearing a nd I will have trouble
staying in here, at that volume.

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I think that message has percolated to those who might
do that.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: In Spain, unemployment has hit 24 percent. The banking
sector is in crisis there, facing serious downgrades and an imminent recession. But this
National Government will not allow that situa tion to happen here. It is through fiscally
responsible policies, pr udent economic management, and sound, common-sense
leadership that we will make this country bolder, brighter, and better again.
So you may ask what this Budget does to balance the books. Well,  we have closed
tax loopholes around livestock and mixed-use assets to save $293 million over 4 years.
We have removed tax credits where they were  no longer serving thei r purpose, and this
will save $117 million. But what is critical is that net core Crown debt will remain
below 30 percent, which is a gold standard compared with other developed countries.
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2837
Significantly, we are reprioritising $4.4 billion over the next 4 years to ensure that New
Zealanders receive better public services in  health, education, so cial services, and
science and innovation. Why are we doing this? We are doing this because these are the
areas that matter to New Zealanders most.
What has been clear in this debate is th e ideological differences between those tired
Opposition benchers and the Government’s aspirational benchers. In a Harvard study,
economists Alberto Alesina and Silvia Ardagna investigated policies aimed at
stimulating the economy in 21 countries,  between 1970 and 2007. Their conclusions
were unequivocal, and I will quote: “Fiscal st imuli based upon tax cuts are more likely
to increase growth than those based on sp ending increases.” They added that spending
cuts are much more effective than tax increases—

items.speaker: Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the member but the time for this
debate has now concluded. I call on the Minist er of Finance, the Hon Bill English, in
reply if he wishes.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: It has been interesting just to hear the
Budget debate wandering along. I must say th at the attitude the Labour Opposition
brought to the House today is pretty much  the one that it has carried throughout the
debate. There is no focus, no real energy, and no sustained intell ectual effort that
illustrates any attempt to get to grips with the way the economic world has changed and
where Budget 2012 fits into that. In fact, you would think with the way the Opposition
turned up to the House toda y that it must have made some announcement a while ago
and then turned round and changed its mind on it. That is what you would think had
happened. I cannot recall an Opposition that was meant to be opposed to a Budget
coming into the House with su ch a weak performance as to day’s. It was unbelievable,
actually, and reflects a kind of lassitude th at can be explained only by the profound
depression the Opposition members must feel at their inability to get a grip on political
debate—

items.speaker: Hon Maurice Williamson
items.text: Resign.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: —as my colleague has sugge sted before, I think, the
Opposition should resign. I can tell you one r eason why that is. The Labour Party, in
particular, and to some extent the Green Pa rty are quite disorientated by the way this
Budget deals with public serv ices. There is a lot of co mmentary about the general
economy, and I can come back to that, but—

items.speaker: Chris Hipkins
items.text: Deals to public services.

items.speaker: Hon BILL ENGLISH
items.text: Well, that is exactly my point—that is exactly my point. The
New Zealand centre-left parties have been waiting around for when the wolf rips off its
sheep’s clothing, sacks half th e Public Service, and shuts the hospitals, and then they
will get their diet of media stories that enab le them to put their feet up and say: “The
world is the way we always thought it w ould be. The nasty Nats don’t care about
anybody. We do, and in the end they’ll vote for us.” It is not happening.
A striking feature of this B udget and the election campaign is that all those people
who at the ballot box act ually do support the Labour  Party are working so
constructively with the Government on publ ic services and on solving our social
problems that we did not hear a word of  criticism—not in the election campaign, and
not around this Budget—with one exception. That was over the pupil-teacher ratio, and
that was so obvious because it was exceptional. [Interruption] Clearly, the member does
not know what Budgets used to be like wh en they were tight. Everybody complained
about everything in the Public Service, but not now, because this Budget includes large
investments in aspects of public services  that the previous Labour Government,
disgracefully, neglected or incompetently messed up.
2838 Budget Debate 12 Jun 2012
But, actually, no one really cares about what Labour did, because there are a whole
lot of people out there constructively e ngaged with the National - John Key - led
Government on, for instance, taking some serious action about long-term welfare
dependency. Labour members wrung their hand s about it while it got worse throughout
the most favourable employ ment conditions in a generation. The centre-left who
support Labour now realise that writing st rategies and wringing your hands does not
work, and they are constructively engaged with  this Government, with this Cabinet, in
major change in how we deal with welfare issues, health issues, and education issues.
I will give just one very simple example,  which is immunisation rates. For 30 years
immunisation rates, particularly among M āori and Pacific childre n, those who need it
most, have been below 70 percent, and to day they are above 90 percent—above 90
percent—not because of strategies, workshops , and consultants but simply because this

items.speaker: Government said
items.text: “We don’t accept that. We think it can be better, and if we tell people
it can be better, they’ll do th e job.” The public health service has done a fantastic job of
lifting those immunisation rates. There is  now no difference in immunisation rates
between P ākehā children and M āori children, even in difficult areas like the Bay of
Plenty. That is just one example. It did not actually take a lot more money, but it did
take some more money.
The other examples are particularly ar ound welfare, where the bankruptcy of the
New Zealand Labour Party is becoming more  obvious by the day. No t a single idea has
it contested around the single biggest allocation of funding in this Budget, which is well
over $250 million to welfare reform—not a word, not a word. The reason is that Labour
has no idea how to deal with it, how to put up a better idea, or how to politically contest
what National is doing. What we are doing is  moving on from the dreadful passivity of
the previous Labour Government, which said: “Because we car e about our most
vulnerable people, we don’t actually have  to do anything to stop them being
vulnerable.” The sneaking suspicion is that wh at drives the Labour Party is that it wants
people to be dependent, because then it n eeds to get them a State house, and it then
needs to have workshops, consultants, and statisticians running a whole industry talking
about it.
This Government believes that people do not need to be vulnerable. They are not
there as fodder for our political machine,  like they are fodder for the Labour Party
political machine. We have committed over a qu arter of a billion dollars in this zero
Budget to doing more to help more peopl e whom we believe can move out of
dependency. The other benefit of it might be that they then stop voting for Labour.
Would that not be fantastic? That would be a real measure of success.
That is why the Budget debate has been a bit lacklustre, because the once-great
Labour Party has nothing to say that is relevant to the issues of the day. Labour
members just harp on with decades-old slogans and hope that somehow we will stuff up
public services enough that th at will feed their political  strategy. It has not happened
despite 4 years of tight Budgets. We will de liver more and better public services for
less, and the delivery system that supports  the Labour Party in the ballot box supports
us—this Government—in the work it is doing and in what it wants to achieve for New
Zealanders who depend on us.
In a context of global uncertainty and a bumpy and slow recovery in the New
Zealand economy, this Budget is a sensible one. It is a sensib le one. It is another step
along the path of rebuilding the growth capacity of this economy, building on the
resilience of so many New Zealanders who ha ve done a fantastic job of adapting to the
way the world has changed. At times they are frustrated and at times they are impatient,
but at all times they are resilient, making th e changes they need to make so they can
secure their jobs, have viable households, get their debt down, and look to the future
12 Jun 2012 Budget Debate 2839
with some aspiration. This Government has never lost its sense of aspiration through
these more difficult times, and we look forward to presenting a Budget next year that
builds further on the aspirations we have for a brighter future.

and the following substituted: “this House has no confidence in this National

First Reading

items.speaker: Hon DAVID CARTER
items.text: I move, That the Local
Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill be now read a first time.  I nominate the Local
Government and Environment Committee to cons ider the bill. At the appropriate time I
intend to move that the Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill be reported to the
House by 15 October 2012.
Can I start by acknowledging the excellent work of my colleague Nick Smith and his
work in developing the Better Local Government reforms.
2840 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 12 Jun 2012
New Zealand’s 78 local author ities are a signif icant component of the New Zealand
economy. They make up 4 percent of GDP, spend $7.5 billion per year of public money,
and manage $100 billion worth of public assets . They deliver a wide range of critical
regulatory functions and local public services that directly impact the lives of New
Zealanders every day. Central government has a part to play in creating an environment
in which local government is better able to contribute to building a more productive and
competitive economy and to deliver better loca l public services. Local government can
then be better positioned to create the envi ronment for local businesses and industry to
emerge and grow, and for communities to fl ourish. This Government’s programme for
reform of the local government sector aims to improve the operation of local
government here in New Zealand. It will focus local authorities on operating more
efficiently and effectively by doi ng things that only they can do. It will deliver settings
that will encourage local authorities to re duce red tape and compliance, minimise rates
for households and businesses, lower their de bt, and provide high-quality infrastructure
at the least possible cost.
The Government’s programme for reform of  the local government sector comprises
two distinct phases. The first phase will refocus the purpose of local government,
introduce financial prudence requirements fo r local authorities, strengthen local
authority governance provisi ons, and streamline local authority reorganisation
procedures. The second phase of the reform programme will consider the report of the
Local Government Efficiency Taskforce, which I announced last week. It will also
develop a framework for the interface betw een central and local government regulatory
roles, investigate the efficiency of local government infrastructure provision, and review
the use of development contributions.
This bill, the Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill, amends the Local
Government Act 2002 to give effect to the first phase of the G overnment’s reform
programme. Firstly, the bill refocuses the purpose of local government. The purpose in
the bill provides for local authorities to meet the current and future needs in their
communities for good quality local infrastr ucture, local public  services, and
performance of regulatory functions in a way that is most cost-effective for households
and businesses. Having a clear and focuse d purpose statement is necessary for the
efficient running of local government in New Zealand.
The second area of reform is the establis hment of financial prudence requirements
for local authorities. In li ne with central government, a nd households and businesses,
councils must restrain spending, keep costs do wn, and run as efficiently and effectively
as possible. In building a more competitiv e and productive economy it is critical that
both local and central government take a pr udent financial appro ach to public money.
This bill provides for regulations to set benchmarks for the prudent overall management
by councils of revenue, expenses, assets, liabil ities, investments, and general financial
dealings.
The bill contains three mechanisms to strengthen local authority governance
provisions. There will be pr ovision for a simpler, more graduated mechanism than is
currently available for central government to  assist struggling local authorities and
intervene before situations become critical. In particular, the new mechanisms can be
used where local authorities are failing, or are close to failing, the new financial
prudence requirements. The leadership roles of mayors will be strengthened in line with
that of the Auckland mayor under the Local  Government (Auckland Council) Act of
2009. Mayors will be given governance powers that  will align with the level of public
responsibility they have for council decisi ons, and that will support clear, strong
leadership by mayors. Elected councils wi ll be specifically enabled to determine
12 Jun 2012 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 2841
policies on staff numbers and remuneration, and they will be required to report annually
on staff employed by salary bands.
The fourth area of reform in the bill is the streamlining of local government
reorganisation procedures for the union, a bolition, and constituti on of districts and
regions, and the creation of unitary authori ties. Currently, such reorganisations can
proceed only if they are supported by more th an 50 percent of the votes cast in each
affected district or region, and reorganisation involves a long and complex process. This
bill will make it easier for communities a nd local authorities to apply for a local
government reorganisation, and it will give  the Local Government Commission more
flexibility in considering applications. Reorga nisation applications will need significant
community support before the commission can progress them.
The Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill is an importa nt milestone in
progressing the first phase of  the Government’s programme for reform of the local
government sector. These reforms are important for New Zealand communities, for
business and industry, and for individual house holds. I believe that these changes will
improve the efficiency and effectiveness of local government a nd provide the right
settings for the local governme nt sector to play its part  in growing the New Zealand
economy. I commend this bill to the House.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: I am standing in for my colleague the
Hon Annette King, and I rise to express Labour’s opposition to the Local Government
Act 2002 Amendment Bill. Labour would support a bill that promotes efficient,
effective, and accountable local government, but this bill is not that. This is a politicised
attack on local government. It will undermin e democratic processes and it takes away
the democratic rights of local communities.
The reforms in this bill are based on a ma nufactured set of statis tics, a selective use
of data by the Hon Nick Smith in a way that has become that former Minister’s
trademark. We saw it earlier in the last pa rliamentary term with his stewardship of
ACC. He whips up a few shonky figures, puts them out into the media, scaremongers up
a good crisis, and then pretends to bring a so lution. That is exactly what happened here,
although it is interest ing to note that  after the data that th ese reforms were based on
were posted on the Department of Intern al Affairs website in a Better Local
Government document, a few days after that document’s release the data was replaced
by the department with a comment saying, and I quote directly from the website: “there
are issues with the data both in terms of accuracy and in terms of the picture that was
being given to some councils.” That is not a very promising start to this Government’s
local government reform agenda, in its second term.
The main issue that I want to speak to in this contribution is about the change to the
rules around the reorganisati on and amalgamation of local councils. Currently, the law
guarantees to all citizens in this country the right to a say in a binding ballot over any
proposed reorganisation or amalgamation of their local council. This bill takes away
that right. It is the confiscation of the democratic rights of New Zealanders, and it opens
the door to forced amalgamations in which th e citizens of the affected areas will risk
having no say at all. Let me  repeat—at the moment, citizen s are guaranteed the right to
have a say. They can vote up or down any amalgamation proposal. What did we see
from this Government in 2009? It circ umvented that right, with the forced
amalgamation in Auckland. What is the Gove rnment doing? It is incorporating that
approach into this piece of law.
If citizens want to have a say, then they  have 40 working days from the time the
organisational change proposal is tabled. They have got 40 working days to get 10
percent of the local voting population to sign a petition seeking the right to have a say in
a binding ballot. That is simply not good enough. This is an assault on the democratic
2842 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 12 Jun 2012
rights of communities all around New Zeal and. It opens the door to forced
amalgamations, and that is a broken promise by this Government.
Last term we heard John Key saying, and we heard other National Ministers saying,
there would be no forced amalgamations. John Key said in March this year, and I quote
from his post-Cabinet press conference: “We think it’s very difficult for communities to
amalgamate, again there’ll be some disc ussions about that wi th the councils to
amalgamate but I wouldn’t look for a forced  situation as you saw in Auckland.” Well,
that is exactly what this bill opens the door to. It takes away the democratic right of
New Zealanders to choose the shape and the scale of their local authorities. It takes
away their right to a binding ballot. That ope ns the door to forced amalgamations. It is
exactly what John Key promised would not happen.
That has become this Government’s modus operandi. We saw it in Auckland, and we
saw it in Christchurch with the sacking of  Environment Canterbury, the removal of the
elected councillors of the Canterbury region. We see that same contempt for democratic
values, the same contempt for our democratic institutions. It is coming through loud and
clear in the Hon Nick Smith’s reform ag enda, brought to the House today by the
Minister of Local Government, David Carter.
There is lots more that is wrong with this bill, and I want to focus on a couple of
other elements. What we see in this bill is  the reincarnation of Rodney Hide’s ludicrous
core services agenda. It survives here in a d iluted form. What it does is it gets rid of the
purpose statement in the current local government  legislation, which is often referred to
as the four well-beings. It replaces that with a narrower focus of providing good quality
infrastructure, plus local public services and regulatory functions, at the least possible
cost to households and businesses. Well, as  many commentators have already pointed
out, this is a nonsense. The regul atory impact statement says this change is  likely to
have a symbolic effect and should not affect council business as usual.
The absurdity of this provision is illustrated by the interview that the Minister gave
on Q+A a few weeks ago. He was asked what sort of council activity he did not approve
of. His example that he gave was the Ham ilton V8 Supercars race. Apparently councils
running V8 races is bad, but the Christchurch flower show—

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: That’s fine.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: That is really good. This illustra tes the absolute intellectual
bankruptcy that underpins this bill. V8 races are out; flower shows are in. So this is the
kind of intellectual rigour, this is the intellectual rigour, that we have come to expect
from this National Government. If Nick Sm ith, who is often touted as having the
biggest brain in the National Cabinet, when he  was in Cabinet, is responsible for this
reform agenda and he is the brightest guy in the National Cabinet, then this country has
got something very serious to worry about.
The Department of Internal Affairs, in th e regulatory impact statement, takes a much
more sober assessment of this issue. It says : “There is no clear quantitative evidence to
suggest that the [Local Government Act 2002]  has resulted in a proliferation of new
activities, or that local government is undertaking a wi der group of functions.” The
regulatory impact statement by the Minister’s own officials contradicts the very premise
that this reform agenda is based on. Nick Smith went around the country saying that the
sky is going to fall, councils are out of cont rol, they are spending here and there, they
are profligate, and the four well-beings have  led to an explosion of council activity
doing all these outrageous things, and that is contradicted by the Minister’s own
officials and the regulatory impact statement.
The other main idea that underpins this bill and this reform agenda is the notion that
council debt is out of contro l, and that councils are racking up more and more debt and
this is a terrible liability. Well, we have  seen from Local Government New Zealand
12 Jun 2012 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 2843
clear evidence that local author ity expenditure as a percentage of GDP is more or less
static at around 3 percent and has been for th e last 5 years. We see that local authority
expenditure as a percentage of total Crown expenditure is more  or less static. In fact, it
has gone down by several points in the last  5 years. The figures show that council
expenditure on interest repa yments as a percentage of  operating income was 4.53
percent in 2010, up from 4.19 percent in 2009. It is  a hardly a crisis. The irony is that at
a time when councils are being diddled out of  a fair share of f unding for local roads,
which for many councils is up to half their operating expenditure, this Government is
beating them with a stick about overexpenditu re when it is cutting back on the funds
that councils rely on just to repair and maintain local roads.
The sinister thing about this Budget is that  it is designed to put the fiscal squeeze on
local authorities at the very time that this Government is trying to  pressure councils in
Auckland, Christchurch, and goodness knows wher e else to sell assets that their
ratepayers have paid for and built up over generations. This Government is trying to do
to local government what  it is doing to central government , and that is to sell off the
family silver and sell off lucrative assets that are owned by the people of those
communities. This is an i llogical, poorly thought-through bill. It takes away the
democratic rights of communities, it underm ines local government, and Labour will not
support it.

items.speaker: NICKY WAGNER
items.text: It is very interesting to
listen to the member Phil Twyford and thin k that there is absolutely no correlation
between what he says and what is happeni ng in the real world out there. He has no
knowledge at all of what is happening globally or in the economy. As the world changes
socially and economically, as new technologies  develop, and as new issues arise, how
we organise our lives, our cities, and our in stitutions needs to change as well. This
Government is introducing th ese local government reforms as part of our focus on
developing a more competitive and more produ ctive economy, because that is what is
going to give us a better future in the long term. We want to use our resources more
wisely. We want to get more for less out of  our institutions and our organisations. We
want to manage our finances better. We wa nt to reduce waste and get better value for
money in everything we do.
The Local Government Act 2002 was supposed to improve local government
management, and we were assured—if you can remember back to 2002—that it would
not add any significant costs, but it did. Over the last decad e rates have become more
and more unaffordable for many more people. In  the last decade, rates increased by an
average of 6.8 percent every year. That is doubl e the rate of inflat ion. Operational costs
have ballooned out. Local government salary co sts are significantly higher than central
government or private enterprise costs. Lo cal government debt has quadrupled from $2
billion to $8 billion. Whatever you say, more debt is bad. It increases uncertainty and
increases liability. While households and businesses are being prudent and
responsible—they have been be lt tightening, they have been  managing their costs, and
they have been paying down debt—local governm ent costs continue to rise. In the face
of global financial pressure and moneta ry uncertainty, ratepayers are becoming
increasingly anxious and concerned about paying their rates and ongoing rate increases.
Ordinary households and businesses have ab solutely no control over rates. They have
no choice but to pay those rates, and they want  to see councils tighten their belts too, as
they have done themselves.
While working on the Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill, local
government Ministers have met with Loca l Government New Zealand, mayors right
across the country, regional c ouncil chairs, regional chie f executive officers, and
numerous ratepayer groups in order to unde rstand the issues and to formulate these
2844 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 12 Jun 2012
amendments. This bill is the first phase of local government reform, but it really focuses
on four main initiatives. The first is to refocus the purpose. It is all very well for Mr
Twyford to say that that will not make a difference, but ratepa yers tell us that what they
want from their councils is re liable and effective infrastructu re, and they want efficient
public service at an affordable cost. That is what they want, so we are going to reword
the purpose to cover that. We are going to say “to meet the current and future needs of
communities”—so current and future, thinking into the future—“for good-quality,” not
rubbish, but good quality, “local infrastructu re, local public servi ces, and performance
of regulatory functions in a way that is  most cost-effective for households and
businesses.” We believe that this will focu s councils on the roles and the duties that are
of most value to ratepayers, but it will st ill allow for individual differences for those
communities.
Ratepayers also tell us that they want the best possible financial management by their
councils, and that makes good sense. We want to introduce consistent financial
prudence requirements acros s local governments, and that means introducing
regulations that will allow for financially prudent parameters and benchmarks. Under
present legislation—the famous 2002 Act by Labour—councils already have to exercise
prudent financial management, and they have to exercise prudent stewardship of their
resources. But if we can develop benchmar ks for this process—and they will be
developed with the consultation of Local Government New Zeala nd—that will allow a
greater understanding for everybody, and greater transparencies in finance for everyone.
Because financial management will be consis tently measured across the country, it will
be far easier to see when a council is out of step or a council is performing poorly, and it
will be far easier to identif y when a council is struggling, and might need Crown
assistance or even require intervention.
Ratepayers also tell us that they want c ouncils, councillors, and mayors to be more
responsible to the people who elect them. We want to strengthen council governance by
giving mayors a stronger leadership role so that  they can have that role over developing
plans, policies, and budgets, and we want to  give them the power to appoint deputy
mayors and also the chairs of committees so that when they go a nd take charge of a
council, they can make sure that what they  have promised can be delivered. We also
want to give more powers to councillors. Wh en you think about it, staffing and salaries
are the major drivers of increased costs in councils. Presently, councils have absolutely
no control over these matters. We  want to make sure that  councils are able to set
employee numbers and salary scales, and we  want them to re port on that salary
information in their annual reports. We believe  that these measures  will make councils
more conscious of the cost and more accountable to the public.
The ratepayers also tell us that they are open to change in the structures of local
government if it gives them better efficien cy. We want communities and councils to
have more flexibility in developing reorganisation proposals. The current process that is
being used is lengthy, it is complex, it is expensive, and it is actually rarely successful—
very rarely. We want to empower communitie s and councils to make changes that have
the potential to achieve effi ciencies and better decisi on-making. The new legislation
will make it easier for the community-led local government reorganisation to succeed,
and it will also give greater flexibility to  the Local Government Commission to develop
reorganisation proposals. There is absolutely no doubt that effective and affordable local
government is essential for the running of every New Zealand household and business. I
think that this amendment bill is designed to provide a better understanding of councils’
roles. It should give us stronger and more  effective governance, improved efficiency,
and more prudent financial management. I commend this bill to the House.
12 Jun 2012 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 2845

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Listening to that member,
Nicky Wagner, I wonder why the Government does not just fold all of local government
up and get Paula Rebstock to run it, becau se that is basically the Government’s
approach to everything at the moment: “Let’s  just corporatise the whole thing, have a
board, and have Paula Rebstock run the whole thing.”
It is important to see this  bill, the Local Government  Act 2002 Amendment Bill, in
the context of what this Gove rnment has done with local g overnment since it got into
office in 2008. It inherited the Royal Commission on Auckland Governance. Everybody
in the Auckland region wanted something to  happen, wanted a more  efficient process,
and wanted better decision-making. The royal commission came through, and this
Government came along and ripped out sections of the report. It just said “No, we don’t
like that bit of it, we don’t like that layer of governance, so we’re going to take that out.
We don’t like the idea that social issues might be dealt with, so we’re going to take that
out, as well.” That was the first step when it came to local government, from this
Government opposite.
Then it moved on to Environment Canterbu ry. The then Minist er responsible for
these things said the Government was not goi ng to have an electi on on that issue. It
would just cancel that, because the Minister  was worried about the outcome. That was
the quote. It was in the Timaru Herald . I remember it well. The former Minister is
nodding. He was worried about the outcome. We ll, I tell you what, I was quite worried
about the outcome of the 2008 general election, but we did not cancel it. We did not say
no, we were not going to have it because we were worried about the outcome. But that
is what this Government did when it came to Environment Canterbu ry. It said to good
people like Eugenie Sage: “I’m sorry, that’s it. You’re out. We’re not going to do this,
because we’re worried about the outcome.”
Well, there is the small matter of democracy. It is a tiny matter that this Government
does not seem at all interested in protecting—certainly not at a local level. Because now
the Government, having tried to disembow el the royal commission report and having
taken out Environment Canterbury, is going to do it to everybody. Satisfied as it is with
what it has done in Auckland and Canterbur y, the Government has come along and said
it is time to get rid of democracy at a local level right across New Zealand.
I want to focus in on the most insidious part of this bill, and that is the fact that the
rights of local residents to have a say on the organisation of the governance in their area
is taken away. The automatic right to a re ferendum is gone, under this bill. Gone! That
is an attack on democracy. That is saying to local residents that they do not
automatically have a right to have a say a bout how they are governed at a local level.
That is wrong. Local people deserve a say in  local decisions. What we now have is a
process by which, yes, a poll, a referendum can  be requested; it has to be requested by
10 percent of the voters in an area. And to  get those 10 percent, the people who are
trying to organise a petition have 40 wo rking days. They have 40 working days from
when a proposal is approved by the Local Government Commission.
In the Wellington region here, should a pr oposal come forward for a so-called super-
city for the Wellington region, that will be around 48,000 signatures to collect in those
40 days. They cannot start any earlier than when the proposa l comes up, and that is as
good as it gets. It is democracy, if you can pull off that 10 percent. It is not democracy
for everybody in the region. It is wrong, and that is an attack on our democracy. This
bill today takes away democratic rights. What  kind of Government comes to this House
to take away people’s demo cratic rights? This kind of  Government does—a National
Government that is determined to see all of local government in the sense of
corporatised, board-like relationships rather than it being part of de mocracy, rather than
it being something that local people have a say in.
2846 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 12 Jun 2012
What we have today in front of us is a bi ll that effectively says that amalgamations
will be coming. “You will get them, no matter what.” Now, some amalgamations may
be a very good idea, indeed. But local people de serve the right to a say, not to have to
go out and work to have a say—they actually deserve a right to ha ve a say about what
the structure of governance will look like in their area. This bill strips that right away.
The word “flexibility” keeps being used, but the question I have got to ask is how we
balance flexibility streamlining against peopl e’s right to have a say in how they are
governed. This bill gets that balance all wrong, and it should not be allowed to pass.
The other part of this bill th at I do want to put some time  into is the question of the
change from the removing the four well-beings from the 2002 Act, because there has
been a lot said about the fact that c ouncils are somehow out of control—that they are
completely out of control with what they are doing as a result of the 2002 Act. To repeat
what Mr Twyford has said, the Department of  Internal Affairs says there is no clear
quantitative evidence to suggest that the Local Government Act 2002 has resulted in a
proliferation of new activities, or that loca l government is undertaking a wider group of
functions. That is the Department of Intern al Affairs. That is the Minister’s own
advisers saying that actually the whole prem ise of that change does not even stack up.
As Mr Twyford said before, frankly, the Government does not even know why it is
changing this particular clause . It wants to look like it is  somehow or other going to
streamline and narrow what it is that local government can do. But the reality is that the
Government does not know. Is it the V8s or is it the flower show?
Now, some people might argue that that is evidence of Maggie Barry’s influence
over this Government—flower shows are in. David Bennett has no influence—V8s are
out. That could be one argum ent for what is driving—[ Interruption]—Tim Macindoe.
Sorry, I forgot. Maggie Barry is in the as cendency; Tim Macindoe and David Bennett
are out. Flower shows versus V8s. But actually I think it is simpler than that. The
Government wants to look like it is making a change in this area, when in reality it is
actually not. But what worries me more is that  this is happening in the context of a time
when the Government, at a central government level, is bailing out of important public
services. It is saying that it is not going to be  providing the kind of  support in housing,
health, and all the areas that we think of as centr al government’s role. Yet at the same
time the Government is trying to tell local government that  it should not be in those
areas either. But it is confused. It does not add up, it does not actually make any sense in
terms of what councils will be directed to do.
And here we have the Auckland Council with its magnificent new plan, founded on
the four well-beings—sorry, not quite sure  we fit into those any more! I have a
prediction: I think they probably will be able to fit everything into the new structure,
because this Government simply does not know what it means by its new purpose
statement for core public services.
The other premise on which this bill flounders  is the fact that the questions around
debt and around the state of councils have not been accurately portrayed by this
Government. Once again, Local Government New Zealand’s figures show that the
average of all councils’ expenditure on interest repayments, as a percentage of operating
income in 2010, was 4.53 percent. Now, it has gone up. It has gone up from 4.19
percent, which is not that big an incr ease. It is a small increase on average.
[Interruption] The former Minister can pick out examples if he likes, but the truth is that
the figures have been beaten up. The figures have been beaten up to try to make the
case, and it does not make the case.
The Auditor-General said that debt levels were well within prudent financial
standards. That is what th e Auditor-General said about local government. Of course
ratepayers want to see good, efficient public  services provided by their councils. Of
12 Jun 2012 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 2847
course they want to make sure, and ther e will be things we can do, but premising
widespread amalgamations forced on loca l people, premising this whole bill on
statistics that do not add up, is not good e nough. The Government needs to be able to
come through with proper proposals—consul ted with the sector —that actually will
improve the way that local government works. There are bits and pieces of it in this bill,
but the reality is that the fundamental cha nges that have been proposed here are anti-
democratic and are based on things that actually do not add up.
But in the end, I want to finish with saying where is all this ending up. Where all this
is ending up is what the Government would like to force local government into doing,
and that is asset sales. It is quite clear that is the agenda. In fact, I do not need to say it.
John Key and David Carter have said it in th e context of Christchurch. They want local
government to shed assets. They want to take the harebrained scheme that this
Government is trying to put in place—in the absence of any kind of real plan for
economic growth—to sell assets, and they want  to transfer that on to local government.
That is wrong. It is wrong in principle, but it is also wrong in pr actice, taking away the
rights from local government to make deci sions, taking away the rights from local
people.
We are opposing this bill, because although there may be  some good streamlining of
local government that could take place, and there may well be good amalgamations out
there that could happen, they should not be  brought about by taking away democratic
rights from people, by taking away the rights of individual citizens to decide how they
are governed. This bill is wrong, and the Labour Party opposes it.

items.speaker: EUGENIE SAGE
items.text: T ēnā koe, Mr Speaker. Local government has an
enormous influence on nature, on our quality of life, on our neighbourhoods, and on the
way our communities function. It has a crucial role in  creating the places and
communities that are safe and pleasant to live, play, work, and retire in.
The Local Government Act was significan tly overhauled and changed in 2002. The
intention then was to empower local communities. Local authorities were intended to be
the instruments of local democracy thr ough which communities achieved the outcomes
they aspired to. This bill winds back that  philosophy. It winds b ack the philosophy of
councils being the instruments of their co mmunities. By changing the purpose of local
government and dropping the requirement to promote the four well-beings, it will
restrict councils to nuts and bolts activities.  This potentially prev ents them from being
the arm around their communities, from unde rtaking activities such as the very
successful Christchurch City Council’s Ki dsFest school holiday programme, or from
providing affordable rental accommodation. As  the regulatory imp act statement on the
Better Local Government discussion pape r notes, there may well be unintended
consequences around changing the purpose of  local government, because that whole
concept of well-being is woven throughout th e principal Act and throughout the whole
framework of local government.
In relation to changing the councils’ purpose, this Local Government Act 2002
Amendment Bill is a solu tion—and a very poorly conceived one—looking for a
problem. That is because section 11A of th e principal Act already requires councils to
“have particular regard to … core servic es … (a) network infr astructure: (b) public
transport services: (c) solid waste collection and disposal: (d) the avoidance or
mitigation of natural hazards: (e) libraries, museums, reserves, recreational facilities
…”. It was not just the regulat ory impact statement that said there was no evidence of a
proliferation of council activities since 2003 ; it was also the re port of the Local
Government Rates Inquiry in 2007.
So the Green Party is opposing this bill. On e of the other reasons is that it takes the
“local” out of “local government ”. It will mean that counci ls are potentially much more
2848 Local Government Act 2002 Amendment Bill 12 Jun 2012
under the thumb and direction of Wellington, and that is because the bill gives the
Minister huge powers to intervene and effectively direct what councils do. So instead of
local councils and central government operatin g in their own spheres, with councils
accountable to local electors,  we will get a very strange hybrid. We will have local
councils that will always have their eye on Wellington and that will be quite nervous of
the Minister intervening through the appointment of Crown observers, Crown
managers, or a Crown review team, or thr ough the ultimate sanction of sacking elected
councillors and replacing them with appointed commissioners.
These ministerial intervention powers concentrate much more power in the
executive. They undermine local autonomy a nd they give the Minister very wide
discretion to intervene, because of the very generous way in which the trigger for
intervention is defined. It is  defined as a “significant pr oblem”, and how is “problem”
defined? It is “a matter or circumstance relating to the management or governance of the
local authority that detracts from, or is likely to detract from, its ability to give effect to
the purpose of local government  within its district or region;”. That allows a huge
amount of subjectivity in the Minister’s decisi on. If it is easier fo r the Minister to get
involved, he or she is more likely to, as the Minister did in Canterbury, and that will cut
across democratic decision-making and it will  cut across the fundame ntal principle of
having no taxation without representation. What is most galling under this bill is that if
the Minister appoints commissioners, it is not central government that pays for them; it
is local electors and local ratepayers who are expected to.
Certainly there have been some well-publicised examples of poorly managed council
expenditure, such as the V8 race in Hamilton and Kaipara’s costly sewerage system, but
