items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: Anyone listening to that speech by the Minister for
Social Development might be under some mi sconception that this bill, the Social
Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amen dment Bill, actually does more than it
does in reality. If this bill was indeed about  removing barriers fo r the large number of
New Zealanders who find themselves in need of Government support right now, I might
be inclined to agree with the Minister, but th at is not what this bill does. In fact, the
Minister even referenced in her speech the number of New Zealanders on the sickness
benefit, in particular, and sa id that unlike the Labour Part y, she was not patting these
people on the head. Not only do I take personal offence to that statement but there is
nothing in this bill that assists anyone on a sickness benefit from illness into wellness
and into work. This bill does not even refe r to people on a sickness or an invalids
benefit. It barely touches them.
So who does this bill affect? The Minister rightly pointed out that she is targeting
young people. “Targeting” is the right word. We have 87,000 young people not in
employment, education, or training—87,000. This bill tackles 1,500 of those young
people. I applaud the Minister. Those are the 1,500 teen parents.
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2867

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: That’s not true. Don’t make up the numbers. You are better
than that. Don’t make up the numbers.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I applaud the Minister for extending childcare payments for
those teen parents, but there are 1,500 of them.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: Come on. You read the facts, and you know it.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: If the Minister thinks ther e are more than 1,500, I would
welcome her tabling that evidence, because th at is the evidence we have received. But
there are 112,000 parents on the domestic pur poses benefit. Now I am coming to the
extra 1,000 on the independent youth benefit—

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: 14,000; you know it works for that many.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: —the extra 1,000. Those young people are being put on a
plastic payment card, and are a number of the select few who will get additional
services from this bill. But there are a vast number more who are locked out by this bill,
because 18 and 19-year-olds will no longer be picked up by services that used to exist
for them. Those are the 14,000 whom the Minist er is speaking about. That is vastly
fewer than the number that Youth Transition Se rvices is currently eligible to pick up. I
am not mixing up the numbers on this bill, Minist er. It is just a fact that there are small
subsets of people who will benefit from it, and not the vast numbers that she refers to.
There used to be a time when we referred not to “welfare” but to “social security”,
and there was a reason for that. In 1938 the unemployment benefit was brought into
New Zealand with the criteria that a person must be 16 years of age and over, have been
in New Zealand for at least 12 months, is unemployed, is capable and willing to
undertake suitable work, and has taken reasonable steps to secure employment. Not a lot
has changed from that criteria, but neither  has much changed about New Zealanders’
desire to work—their absolute desire to be in work. We acknowledge on this side of the
House that whenever you bring in a universal  system, there will be a small minority of
people who will abuse it. It is exactly the same  for the tax system in New Zealand. It is
a universal system that is abused by a minor ity of people, and just  like we must deal
with those who abuse the tax system, we mu st deal with those who abuse the welfare
system. But we must never allow ourselves  to be guided by the minority when we
legislate around the majority. That is wher e I want to bring a few facts into the
discussion.
The Minister is right to compare the di fference in unemployment numbers that we
have in this country. At the beginning of 2008 we had, roughly, almost 18,000 on an
unemployment benefit. Now it is closer to 50,000. We have not had a sudden and
dramatic change in attitude to work; we have had a recession.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: What’s happened in the last 2 years?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: We have had an economic downturn, and I acknowledge that,
Minister, but that is a reflection of the fact that New Zeala nders have not made a choice
to be on welfare and to be on unemployment benefits. That is why we must focus on the
economy if we want to turn round welfare.
Secondly, let us actually use some of the evidence we ha ve got from those who are
on different forms of benefits. The Inland Re venue Department did a survey of those
who have been on the benefit, and found that 64 percent said that they did not have the
skills they needed to get into the jobs that they were trying to get themselves into. The
Government, in this bill, has not done anything to address the fact that so many of those
who are on Government support right now do not have the skills and education
necessary to move into those jobs. Instead, it changed the criteria to the training
incentive allowance. It cut out vast swathes of women, in particular, who were trying to
access education to better themselves in the workplace.
2868 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
I have an example of the kinds of policy that mean that people are not able to get into
sustainable, long-term employment. I recently had a domestic purposes benefit recipient
approach my office and tell me this story. She had been in work for a couple of years
when she found herself pregnant. She had a t oddler when her partner decided he did not
want to be a father and left her. She managed to find work—10 hours a week in
hospitality—but was still on Government support,  and did not want that for her or her
child. She went to Work and Income a nd asked whether there was any assistance
available so she could get into foundation courses to become a nurse—the kind of job
that would get her off the benefit in th e longer term. And do you know what Work and
Income told her? Work and Income told her that she would not be eligible under its
criteria because she had work—because she had 10 hours’ work a week and was still
reliant on Government support. That is the ki nd of system that leaves people trapped in
our welfare system, rather th an offering them the opportunity  to get into sustainable,
long-term work that gives them and their child a better future.
The Inland Revenue Department also found that 67 percent of those on welfare had a
problem getting work that paid enough, a nd 66 percent could not get enough hours.
That makes it sound like those parents, in pa rticular, who are on the domestic purposes
benefit, which is roughly 112,000 at the mome nt, are making a choice to stay on that
benefit because they are better off. Let us just look at the facts. The average amount that
someone on a domestic purposes benefit gets  before an accommodation supplement is
$288 a week for them and their child—$288 a wee k. If we have parents in this country
who are finding themselves not better off going  into work, when they are getting only
$288 a week on the benefit, that suggests that  there is something vastly wrong with our
system—and there is. Actually, the Minister ha s acknowledged it in the bill, and that is
childcare costs. The Minister has acknowle dged that by saying that she is going to
extend the child support payment for teen parents from the $3.91 they are currently
eligible for, to $6.

items.speaker: Hon Paula Bennett
items.text: Would you take away the $80 million?

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: I applaud the Minister for doing that. She does not want to
hear praise. She is barracking across the other side of the House, rather than listening. I
do applaud the Government for improving child support for those teen parents. But that
is 1,500 young people. There are 112,000 DPB recipi ents who are not eligible for that
extension and support and who th erefore still struggle to fi nd jobs that will cover the
costs of caring for their child. This has to be  about making it a viable option to get back
into work. That means making sure our pare nts have the skills and education, and that
we also look to the real barriers to them getting back into the workplace. And we cannot
ignore the costs of childcare and support in looking at that basic issue.
But let us not forget the basic fact that 65 percent of people on the DPB come off it
within 4 years. They come off it as soon as  they are able to im prove their childcare
arrangements, and that is because, of course, 20 hours of early childhood education cuts
in at about that point. If we could do more  to improve that accessibility, what a vast
difference we would make for the number of parents who are reliant on Government
support at the moment. This has to be a deba te based on fact and a debate based on the
reality of what the people whom we are deba ting here are talking about in their day-to-
day lives. That means it has got to be about work, and it has to be about addressing
those real barriers.
I will acknowledge that there are one or two examples of that in this bill, but, by and
large, there are not real examples that will make a major difference to the majority of
New Zealanders who find themselves on social security in New Zealand. I challenge the
Government to turn round its approach to we lfare to being not one of social shame but
one truly of social security.
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2869

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: I rise to support the second
reading of the Social Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill. It is a
pleasure to support Minister Bennett and Prim e Minister Key in bringing these reforms
to the House. These changes, as the Minist er for Social Development has pointed out,
are well overdue. We know that 13 percen t of our working-age population are on a
benefit. We know that we spend more than $7 billion on benefits annually, and that is
$20 million per day, or $67,000 for the time it wi ll take me to give this speech.
Critically, we know that 220,000 Kiwi kids gr ow up in benefit-dependent homes. We
know that long-term welfare dependency is failing our families and their kids. This
National Government, behind Minister Bennett , is standing up and saying that we are
going to do something about it. We believe th at those who can work should work. But
we know that those seeking work sometimes  need encouragement and support. These
welfare reforms will provide that. Crucially, we believe that those who are in genuine
need of assistance—those whom Ms Ardern talks about—will receive welfare going
forward.
So how does the Government achieve this? Well, it does it by investing into the
future of our families—the lifeblood of our communities—for the benefit of our nation.
Budget 2012 provides an upfront investment of $287 million to support more long-term
beneficiaries into work.
Le’aufa’amulia Asenati Lole-Taylor: Going forward?

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: That is right. It is about facts, as Ms Ardern asked. The
facts are that $80 million will go into early childhood education childcare. More facts—
$55 million will go into front-line services to assist job seekers and sole parents into
work. More facts—$149 million will go into wr aparound services, which I will come to
later in this speech.
So what does this bill do to help peop le into work? Well, it places on young people
receiving the new youth payment, or young pa rent payment, obligations to improve
their educational and social outcomes. Th ese changes, though, are not merely about
reform; they are about changing the focus, at titude, and behaviour of those on welfare.
This will have a greater emphasis on wor k, and support those people in every way to
achieve their own dreams and aspirations, and th at of their families. It is about getting
behind people. [Interruption] That is right. It is about ge tting behind people so that they
can realise what they can do, not what they cannot do, as Ms Ardern keeps pointing out.
Resources will be available, particularly to those who are at risk of long-term welfare
dependence. Young people will be supported to make better choices: to stay in
education, training, or work. They will be provided with financial incentives.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Nobody believes this.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: That is what this bill do es, Mr Prasad. They will be
provided with financial incentives to utilise budgeting services and parenting
programmes. These are part of the wraparound services and assistance for those
receiving benefits.
We are no longer just going to hand over benefits like the Labour Government did,
and leave people to their own devices. Instead , we are going to take an active, work-
based approach, because we have greater aspirations for New Z ealanders and their
children than that lot did. This is achieved through hard work and not welfare. We want
people to stand and support themselves, to make good decisions that affect their lives
positively. We will be there to encourage a nd support them. So this welfare programme
will put a clear emphasis on work availabil ity and preparation requirements for those
who can work. This will affect sole parents, widows, women alone, and partners by
requiring sole parents with children aged 5 y ears and over to be av ailable for part-time
2870 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
work. It will also require so le parents with children aged 14 and above to be available
for, and seek, full-time work.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Where is the evidence this works?

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: But what it does—and Mr Prasad knows this, but he
denies it—is provide clear expectations a nd obligations. It is a genuine partnership
between the State, on one side, and those who receive State assistance.
So what do these reforms look like in practic e? Last year I met a young lady of 18 in
my electorate of Maungakiekie. She ha d an 18-month-old baby and was heavily
pregnant with another child. She was living in a cold, damp gara ge, and finding it hard
to make ends meet. She and her family had literally—literally—fallen through the
cracks, and they were living in squalor. Under these new reforms we will be supporting
this young woman with income support, budgeting, parenting services, and access to
training and education.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Ha, ha! It’s there now.

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Mr Prasad might laugh. He might laugh, but despite his
protests this young lady and her children will welcome the assistance that this
Government will provide her, going forward.
Finally, you hear Mr Prasad, Mr Sio, a nd others across the Chamber asking where
the jobs are. I will tell them where the jobs are. The latest household labour force survey
shows that more people are being employed in this country than ever before. In March
2012 there were 2,230,000 employed. That is more than at any time in our history. This
is 30,000 more people employed than when this  Government took office in November

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: How many are out of work?

items.speaker: Peseta SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: Do your research, Mr Pras ad. The SEEK website today
had over 16,000 jobs available online—12,800 full-time, 900 part-time, and over 2,000
for contract positions.
As I conclude this speech, I say once again to these members opposite, and the
people who are listening out there in New Zealand, that these changes are long overdue.
They will bring this welfare system into m odern times. I want to congratulate the Prime
Minister and Minister Bennett once again. They have tack led the very difficult issues
facing our society with compassion and care.  These measures will make this country
bolder, brighter, and better again. I know that the people  in Maungakiekie and New
Zealanders across this land are ready for these changes.  I welcome them. Long term,
these changes will move people out of welfare and into employment. That is good for
their families. That is good for our communitie s, and, yes, it is of great benefit to our
country. I urge all members of this House, right across this House, including our Green
friends over here, to support this Governme nt in bringing about these changes. I
commend this bill to the House.
Su’a WILLIAM SIO (Labour—M āngere): I think that last presentation by the
member Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga reflects the h eartless attitude of th is Government. I can
say to that member that he is not going to  return to Parliament in 2014. This Social
Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill introduces a significant
shift in the direction of welfare reform, and will have an immediate impact on the well-
being and welfare of many low-income individuals and families. The Government’s
reform will have an immediate impact on the financial and emotional future of those
being targeted by this Government—namely, young people and sole parents.
The greatest concern for me is that it will ha ve the most severe effect on the lives of
children who belong to families living in pove rty, or living below the poverty line. As
the Children’s Commissioner submitted at the submission stage, this bill makes no
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2871
requirement to take up the best interests of the child or children affected by these
reforms. It does not take into consideration the best interests of the children.
Labour opposes the reform contained in this bill. These reforms are poorly designed,
they are confusing, they lack safeguards, a nd they destroy trust in our young people. As
the Salvation Army submitted, the bill is funda mentally inconsistent with the intention
of the Social Security Act. I agree with  the Women’s International League for Peace
and Freedom, which submitted that this bill discriminates on human rights in terms of
age, gender, and employment status. I believe it when Women’s Health Action said that
it gave a comprehensive submission based on evidence opposing this bill because, it
said, it undermines women’s sexual and reproductive human rights.
We know from the evidence, which is so read ily available, that child poverty exists
now in New Zealand. We also know from the evidence that child poverty increases
when there is rising unemployment and ri sing underemployment. That has happened
throughout the 4 years that this Government ha s been in power, the consistent trending
of rising unemployment and rising underemplo yment. We also know that when more
people are working part-time or casual jobs there is more poverty. When families have
low incomes relative to living costs there is  a larger gender wage gap, and women who
choose to become mothers are often penalised in the workforce, as they are now under
the current environment created by this Government. There is increasing child poverty.
We also know from evidence that when Gove rnments cut benefits or limit eligibility
for benefits, or have lower income taxes and introduce higher goods and services taxes,
these policies also increase child poverty. Th is is the current economic environment
upon which this Government is  introducing these significant changes to New Zealand’s
social security system.
Every group or individual that I heard submit was quite scathing of the collapsed
process with which this Government drove th e introduction of this bill. It gave very
little time to individuals and organisations to prepare submissions. According to the
Law Society there were groups that could not submit because of the Government’s
collapsed approach to public submissions. The Council of Trade Unions probably best
summed up the feelings of submitters when it said that the Government makes a
mockery of democracy when it rams through significant changes in such a short time
frame, which limits public contribution.
The Government reforms target young people and sole parents. We were advised that
it is the expectation of this Government that when these young people reach the age of
18 years, they will be in employment and will no longer require a benefit. I find that
very difficult to believe, given that the approach is more of a big stick than a carrot. But
even if the carrot was accepted, what jobs are available to people? Many submitters
questioned the Government about where the jobs are. They que stioned what this
Government was doing to enab le the creation of genuine, meaningful, and high-value
jobs that pay well for workers and thei r families. Dr Robin Gwynn submitted that
having people work instead of just accepting money is an excellent idea, but it will not
succeed unless there are jobs for people. He also asked the same question every other
submitter asked about where the jobs are, and said that if the Government believes it has
the right to bully people into work, it should also ensure that jobs exist for people.
Under the Government’s bill sole parents will be required to find part-time work
when their youngest child is 5 years old. They  will be expected to find full-time work
when their youngest child is 14 years or ol der. These changes w ill apply to women
receiving the widows benefit,  domestic purposes benefit, and the domestic purposes
benefit for women alone. It is expected that  56,300 people with children under 5 will be
forced to find work. We were advised that  45,000 people with child ren aged 5 to 14
years will be pushed towards fi nding full-time or part-time work. We were advised that
2872 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
21,300 people with children aged 14 years, or who do not have children, will be pushed
to have full-time work. Sanctions will apply if people fail to meet these expectations.
The Government wants to introduce this bill in July. The CCS Disability Action
submitted that this bill does not address barri ers of single parents with disabled children
forced to enter the workforce. The We llington People’s Centre pointed out to
Government MPs that job matching was a hu ge issue and that many solo mums or
widows were on casualised part-time work, receiving wages that ensured that they
struggled continually to make ends meet. Ka y Brereton was lost for words to describe
the absurdity of the Government’s bill dicta ting that if you have a child you will not get
a benefit. The Women’s International Leag ue for Peace and Freedom said that paid
work is not more important than the “unpaid  work of child rearing and caring for those
in need,”. Graham Howell submitted and said that this bill “smacks of social
engineering of the worst kind” and is flawed from a conceptual and practical basis. He
further said—this was Mr Ho well—that the changes will  “increase the number of
jobseekers, all … bidding for low-waged jobs”, thus driving down wages.
Dr Anita Lacey of Auckland Action Against Poverty said the bill  “does nothing to
address the real causes of poverty in New Zealand, which include a poorly performing
economy, low wages, a shortage of decent jo bs, benefits that are too low for many
people to live on, and … job insecurity”.  The Auckland Women’s Centre showed
evidence that showed that women affected by this bill are already under-resourced.
They live in poverty, have bad health, and need  to be supported, rather than be bullied
by this Government. The Auckland Women’s Centre opposes the bill and describes it as
mean-spirited and punitive. It said women sh ould be supported and given real choice,
not compelled or bullied by this Government.
Labour believes that, by and large, New Zeal anders want to wor k. This is supported
by the evidence that we have seen in th e household labour force survey. Not only the
thousands of people who line up whenever ther e are jobs available in supermarkets but
also the thousands of New Zealanders w ho are leaving our shor es every week for
Australia are clear evidence th at this Government is taking this country in the wrong
direction. We believe that t hose currently in need of Government support deserve a set
of measures grounded in evidence and the reality of the current economic environment.
People require a set of measures that addr ess the barriers that exist in moving from
the welfare system and into work. They dese rve to be treated with dignity, as human
beings deserving of the means to support a nd sustain themselves and their families.
People need jobs. People want to work. People want to earn an income that gives them
dignity as a human being to support their children. The reforms introduced by this
Government treat people with disrespect, or treat them as not hing less than what people
are demanding.
I now want to conclude. The behaviour of the chair and some members of the Social
Services Committee during th e public submissions stage was appalling—appalling.
Aided and abetted by that chair, they consistently challenged submitters. They
consistently undermined submitters, given the collapsed framework that the public had.
I would say that this Government is taking us in the wrong direction.

items.speaker: JAN LOGIE
items.text: It will come as no surprise to anyone in this House, I suspect,
that the Green Party will be voting against this bill, the Social Security (Youth Support
and Work Focus) Amendment Bill, tonight. We oppose this bill for many reasons, many
of which were just listed by my colleague Su’a William Sio. They reflect the concerns
of the people and organisations  that got their submissions in but also those that we
consulted directly because we were not satisfied that 10 days  to get in submissions was
long enough. I will be sharing some of those comments directly this evening.
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2873
The Green Party does not believe welfare is all about the individual, and our belief is
based on several pieces of evidence. Be tween 1999 and 2008 the number of people on
the unemployment benefit plummeted fr om 161,000 to 17,000 because the economy
was doing better. The number of young girls having babies is trending down, without
Government intervention. The proportion of so le parents with jobs  has increased since
the 1990s, and has started levelling off only as job growth has slowed.
Most people on the DPB are on it for a very limited period of time. Less than 10
percent of current recipients  have received the DPB continuously for 10 years or more.
We also know that there ar e really significant and valid, actually, reasons for people
needing the DPB. A large percentage of wo men accessing the DPB do so for reasons of
domestic violence, and CCS Disability Acti on told us during submissions that 25.8
percent of people on the DPB have children with  disabilities whom they are caring for.
There have also been numerous pieces of re search in this country  that have clearly
demonstrated discrimination in the job ma rket, especially based on race, age, and
ability. All of this evidence speaks to structur al issues that will not be addressed by this
legislation.
Although the Green Party rejects the indi vidualistic approach, for the reasons
mentioned above, I do understand that, at le ast, it is a consistent philosophy for the
National Party, even if it is not supported by all the evidence. But in the words of the
feminist icon John Armstrong, National appear s to have one rule for women and no
rules for men. Mr Key said last year 4,300 ch ildren were born to mothers on a benefit—
a shockingly high figure, 4,300—so this Govern ment is changing the law to try to stop
this, changing the law in a way that will potentially take mothers away from their babies
once they are 1 year old. Yet all the while the Government is not doing anything to
track down the estimated 30,000—yes, 30,000—or so fathers who have left it to the
State to pay for the upbringing of their children, l eaving us with a debt of $2.3 billion.
In the words of a woman who has used th e services of Women’s Refuge: “I’ve a
$30,000 debt from studying a level 4 course . My ex has reduced child support to
nothing, while he continues to travel around th e world and tell the kids he doesn’t have
any money because he’s giving it all to me. My ex is on over $120,000 and honestly
thinks he’s poor. I honestly don’t think they know what it’s like not to have $3 to buy
milk, or to have your phone cut off because you can’t pay the bill, what it’s like to have
to go through the systems and beg just to l ook after your kids.” For this House to be
considering easing up on child  support payments while in creasing work testing for
women on the DPB and cutting the training incentive allowance for higher-level courses
is a validation of that man’s disproportionate sense of entitlement.
Several submitters through the submission period spoke about the punishment of
beneficiaries and the stigmatisation. John Key and the Minister for Social Development
have said that beneficiaries need a kick in  the pants, that beneficiaries are living a
dream, choosing a lifestyle, and have to us e a food bank only because they are making
poor choices or do not know how to budget. These comments, alongside the vilification
and misrepresentation of beneficiaries who da re to put their name  to their concerns,
create the context of this bill. This lifest yle or dream has been described by one of the
women I spoke to: “When I left”—a violen t relationship—“I looked online for forms
and information and went in. But it turned out I hadn’t filled in the right forms or didn’t
have the right ID, or something, so I had to  get another appointment. That happened so
often. It’s really humiliating and demoralis ing sitting, waiting, always waiting, then
having to tell a random person your story in fr ont of the whole office. The other day I
was telling my story again and the woman next  to me was saying ‘O h, that’s terrible!
They really have to give it to you.’ That was nice, but sometimes you just don’t want
everyone knowing your story.” That is the dream.
2874 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
The new model of a wraparound service fo r young people is promising a lot—except
jobs—but in the words of a young woman who used the independent youth benefit
recently: “I have friends who go to places and they promise, promise, promise, and then
more people come in, and they forget, and my friends just get lost.” Although tying
funding to outcomes may be a motivator for th e organisations to get their act together,
this is really specialised work, and trust is particularly hard to build, especially when
you are going to have to report the young pers on to Work and Income if they do not
comply. In the words of another young woma n who knows: “Service providers need to
take time to get behind the front. We lear n to have a front to be tough. Once you cut
their benefit they’ll just get more gangster— more crazy. More crime is going to happen
for sure. You can always swap your food card for drugs, and smokers will just go to the
dairy and steal them.”
The Green Party agreed with the presen ters who wanted to see the successful
schemes, like the one in Ōtorohanga and Southland’s Work ’n it Out, replicated. We
believe in investing in young people. Rather th an create a whole new scheme that is not
grounded in evidence, and that creates ethical challenges that have meant that a lot of
respected providers have not applied for c ontracts, we would re plicate the programmes
that work.
Another submitter talked about the difficu lties created by the payment cards. They
worried about the extra leve l of bureaucracy being placed  between a young person and
finding a new place to live, when their flatting situations are often pretty unstable, and
the mixed message that a payment card  sends by locking young people into more
expensive shopping options compared with farmers’ markets or second-hand stores,
while supposedly teaching them good financial management.
Other youth workers and the Children’s Comm issioner raised concerns about setting
National Certificate of Edu cational Achievement level 2 as the benchmark. For young
people who have been out of the school syst em for long periods of their life—and some
of them have not ever been in it, from be ing refugees—this is likely to be demotivating,
to say the least.
Young mothers and other submitters all rais ed concerns regarding the lack of
availability of appropriate courses in ch ildcare. Along with numerous submitters, we
reject the view that parenting is not valu able work. In the word s of another woman:
“And, honestly, monitoring and caring for a t eenager can be a full-time job. I am
actually really frightened about going back to work. Even my parents, who are very
conservative, anti-welfare, churchgoing people have told me I need to stay off work.
They said—which hurt at the time—that ‘You’ve been so focused on managing your
relationship for the last 13 year s that your kids haven’t had the love and attention that
they’ve been waiting for.’ If I worked, I’d  have some more money, but no time. The
kids need anger management counselling, and help with managing their father, as well
as just some focus.”
The drivers for welfare are many and complex, and so the answers need to be
comprehensive. The Green Party is ambitious enough to believe that we can work
together with business, lo cal government, and community  to create a productive
economy that, in turn, feeds an inclusive society.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: I was just wondering whethe r we were sitting in this
House listening to this debate on the Social  Security (Youth Support and Work Focus)
Amendment Bill or listening to a drama unfolding, and I was about to fall asleep. It was
a soothing voice, however. I commend Jan Logi e for the voice; it was a very soothing
voice to fall asleep to.
This is my first opportunity to speak on th e bill, and I have to wonder whether those
members opposite were sitting in the same select committee as I was, because they
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2875
obviously have a completely different view of what actually happened in the select
committee room. So I would like to take th is opportunity to commend the tremendous
work that the Minister for Social Development, the Hon Paula Bennett, has actually
done. The previous Labour Government in 9 years did not have the guts to actually
tackle—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order! Using that term is not
acceptable.

items.speaker: MELISSA LEE
items.text: Thank you. What I was about to sa y was that our Minister has the
courage to tackle something that the Labour Government did not have.
When the architects of the welfare system  set about designing how it was actually
going to work, they would never have imagined that we would have 220,000 children
growing up in welfare-dependent homes, or that 170,000 people would have been on
welfare for most of the last decade. What  welfare was designed for was to provide a
safety net for people in difficult times, and it is still so. But in New Zealand we have
long-term welfare dependency, which is tr apping many people into a life of limited
choice, poverty, and poor health. We all agree across this House that we need to actually
do better, and that is what this Government is doing.
We know that often when people enter into the welfare system at a younger age, they
tend to stay on welfare for much  longer, and that is a fact. So for me, we must provide
an environment where these young people who would otherwise have very limited
choice going into welfare have a choice for a better life outcome a nd a brighter future.
By identifying these at-risk yout h, we can provide se rvices to help them re-engage with
education, training, and opportunities for employm ent, and this bill sets out to do just
that.
This bill will deliver a more effective a nd active welfare system with greater support
for our young people, as aspects of our current  welfare system are out of step with
modern life—for example, the widows bene fit and women alone benefit. The current
welfare system simply pays benefits to young people and teen parents and, effectively,
leaves them to it. That is what the Labour Government did. Well, that is just not good
enough. Often these young people do not have the life skills or the experience to know
how to budget or prioritise, or to understand that  education is what is required for a
better outcome. They need good role models  and advice on how they can best make
things work for them.
This bill will provide a youth and young parent payment, and a youth support
provider will work with them to get them back into education and training. The support
provider will actually manage the young person ’s benefit payments, with essentials like
rent and power paid directly, and an allowa nce and payment card for living costs. Most
of us know how to pay mortgage payments or rent or power on automatic payments,
because those are the essentials that we cannot spend from our pay packet. We know
how to apportion it. Young peopl e do not tend to, and we need  to actually teach them
how to do that. This is a great bill and I commend it to the House.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR (NZ First) : I rise on behalf of New
Zealand First—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: Nice blue scarf.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : —yes, a very nice blue—just to
remind people on the other side who the real traditional national party is. I rise on behalf
of the New Zealand First Part y, the party that takes pride in its common sense and its
realistic approach to social services po licies. In fact, the Minister for Social
Development would do well to seek quality a dvice from New Zealand First, and we are
happy to offer that advice.
2876 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
I am somehow stunned by the previous sp eaker Melissa Lee’s poor contribution on
this debate. Screaming through the microphone does not necessarily represent quality, I
must say.
Let us be real here. The aim of the Soci al Security (Youth Support and Work Focus)
Amendment Bill is to transform the benefit system into one that is modern, active,
work-focused for adults, and education-fo cused for young people. And, yes, Mr Lotu-
Iiga, New Zealand First continues to ask the question of where the jobs are. Where are
the jobs, at the end of the day? Has the Government received funding from the
Australian Federal Government for these proposed training programmes? Because we
can be sure that it will be benefiting from  them. Our tertiary students at present are
already on one-way tickets across the Ditch and to other parts of Europe and Asia, while
the Government shows no intention at all of  holding on to them. Instead, the Minister
proposes to boost a growing exodus.
In fact, New Zealand is becoming an excelle nt employment agency, or shall we say
training institution, for Australia. Perhaps we should ask Australia to thank the New
Zealand National Government for doing this. I recall—

items.speaker: Mike Sabin
items.text: They’re upskilling their mining to come home to Northland.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR: —let me remind Mr Mike Sabin—a
former Prime Minister of a National Govern ment who once said that New Zealanders
who emigrate to Australia raise the IQ of both countries. Sadly, nowadays they raise the
IQ of Australia and other countries but not New Zealand.
Pushing this bill forward suggests speedy implementation of legislation that
hopefully does not come under close scrutiny. Yes, we believe that reducing long-term
welfare dependency is something that th is Government needs to address. We
acknowledge that, but where within these schemes does it provide the solutions?
“Where?” is the question. I can  tell everyone in this House and those who are listening
to this debate now what this bill is a solution to. This bill is merely a concealment. It is
this Government’s disguise of a job creat ion scheme for bureaucracy—in other words,
sugar coating. It is sugar coating, which is probably the more relevant term.

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: For what?
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : That is right, Mr Tim Macindoe.
New Zealand First is concerned about a number  of changes proposed in this bill. These
include the use of the private sector in finding jobs, information-sharing provisions
within the bill, the wider welfare reform p ackage, and, of course, the cost to the
taxpayer. Furthermore, we see the bill as  a distraction from the Government’s poor
economic management and its failure to provide the right setting for job creation.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: She’s right, there.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : That is right. Thank you. I agree
with you, and I thank you for agreeing with me . Looking at the current benefits that
people have access to—namely, the independent youth benefit—I see the same
expectations laid out for 16 to 17-year-olds.  There are the same obligations to be met
regarding secondary schooling, full-time trai ning, and activeness in looking for work. I
see exactly the same frameworks surrounding a youth benefit but with a difference in its
title and its opening, yet again, for political cronyism.
If we look at this bill from its intent, on stating the obvious, it exceeds all levels. You
can laugh about it, Mr Lotu-Iiga, but we discussed this at the Social Services
Committee, and we made our view pretty clear. Yes, it has outlined that better parenting
education programmes and budgeting progra mmes are needed for young parents. But
where are your figures to say how much this  will cost New Zealand taxpayers? Where
are the figures? What we do not want is the transfer of beneficial funds—
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2877

items.speaker: Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I can help this new,
inexperienced member with the figures. I am quite happy—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, you are interrupting the
member’s speech.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : I can sympathise with that member,
because he perhaps needs a little bit more education about when to stand up and call a
point of order. The benefit system should actively help and prom ote paid work and
independence, not create barriers to fi nding paid work. As my colleague Barbara
Stewart once said—

items.speaker: Tim Macindoe
items.text: How does this bill do that?
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : Are you listening, Tim Macindoe?
Are you listening? I am trying to remind you of what was discussed in the select
committee, just in case you have a memory problem there. As my colleague Barbara
Stewart stated in her speech, Treasury has “provided a job forecast of 1.6 percent per
annum over the next 3 years.” She made that  very clear. The question, though, is what
sort of jobs we are talki ng about here—what sort of j obs. Since the Government has
deceived its voters into believing that jobs w ould be available, there are now more job
losses. I can infer only that this forecast is based on optimism, which is far different
from reality.
The information-sharing section, proposed section 125D in clause 19, screams of a
nanny State, which the National Government  has actually accused Labour of doing.
This bill permits certain agencies to disclose information about young persons in certain
circumstances. Who, then, decides which rele vant agencies have access? I definitely
cannot imagine Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga to be someone who can give that. Who are these
intended agencies—or can I say buddies—and  what are the certain circumstances?
Under proposed new section 125D there is no explanation given as to which
organisation will have accessibility rights, and which individuals will have their
information shared. We find no problem with  the Ministry of Education providing
information to the Ministry of Social Development—that is absolutely fine. This is with
reference to the provision relating to th e use of the National Student Number—we
recognise that. In respect of the provision relating to the use of the National Student
Number, though, we will support the inclusi on of a specific provision concerning
information sharing between the Ministry of  Education and the Ministry of Social
Development. We agree, however, with the Privacy Commissioner that the changes in
this bill target a group in whom trust in authority may already be in short supply. That is
very important to note.
Modern society norms are what this Gove rnment wants to align its models with.
Really? Is it normal to ask widows and wo men living alone to take on board work,
without taking into considera tion their circumstances? Is th e Minister saying that the
norm of this Government is to be insensitive to these women and widows?

items.speaker: Kris Faafoi
items.text: Yes.
Le’aufa’amulia ASENATI LOLE-TAYLOR : Yes, I believe so. Women, for as
long as we can remember, have always had an  important role in our community and in
our families. For women alone in the 50- plus age group, where does the Government
propose these women find jobs? It is hard enough for youth to find jobs. And what do
you say about the older generation’s prospects in this competitive job market?
New Zealand First opposes this bill, and the reason we oppose it is that it does not
make sense. New Zealand First said from its  very beginning that we will support good
legislation and oppose bad legisla tion. If the intent of  this bill actually served a purpose
in reducing welfare dependency and gave a real solution to this problem, we may have
2878 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
had a different stance. However, for these legitimate reasons, New Zealand First will
not support the amendment bill in its second reading. Thank you.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: When I spoke in the first reading
debate on this bill, the So cial Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment
Bill, I made the comment that the issue we are talking about is probably the greatest
challenge of our political generation. I also made the point that I believe the outcome of
this bill will be one of the defining achievements of the John Key - led Government.
Jacinda Ardern earlier tonight misrepresented the figures that this bill will cater for,
so I want to clarify that we are talking about 14,000 young pe ople, aged 16 or 17 years,
who are not in employment, education, or training. Not a few hundred, but 14,000. They
deserve our help and our guidance, and, most of all, they deserve a future. But they
cannot do it on their own or with the soft bigot ry of low expectations that characterises
the approach over many years of members opposite in this House.
I am very proud to be a member of the So cial Services Committee, and I will be
especially proud when the benefits of this measure bear fruit, as they undoubtedly will.

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: Will you resign if they don’t?

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Opposition members, like Dr Prasad, are stuck in a time warp.
And those members ignore reality—tragically, not  at their own peril, but at the peril of
those whom they claim to represent, an d whose interests th ey are unquestionably
failing. I endorse 100 percent the outstandi ng work of our Minister for Social
Development, Paula Bennett.  She is doing a fine job and a tough job, and I commend
her for that. I endorse 100 per cent the excellent work of the chair of th e Social Services
Committee, Peseta Sam Lotu-Iiga, who, I ha ve to say, has handled  the whole process
with dignity, with courtesy, with respect, with  intelligence, and with fairness. And I put
that on the record because I have been appall ed at the attacks on hi s character tonight.
He is a fine man doing a very fine job. I al so commend the excellent work of the very
fine deputy chair, Melissa Lee. I am proud to  stand shoulder to shoulder with all three
of those members of this House, and I back their effort 100 percent. Let us get on with
the job.
Contrast their efforts and th eir contributions in this debate with the ideological
claptrap of the Opposition speakers. Su’a William Sio accused the MP for
Maungakiekie of being heartless. That was the word he used. Well, I say to Mr Sio that
I take offence at, and exception to, that clai m. Mr Sio should be ashamed of making it,
because throwing young people into the too-ha rd basket and patronising them with
welfare without expectations is what is rea lly heartless. That is the bigotry of low
expectations that characterises the me mbers opposite. Michael Joseph Savage, the
architect of the modern welf are State, would be utterly appalled. What Labour oversaw
in the first years of this decade is so far removed from what Michael Joseph Savage and
his colleagues envisaged and intended when they established the modern welfare system
that I am sure that he and they would disown their successors on that side of the House.
Mr Sio also attacked the select committee process. Well, as I said, it was a very well-
run process, and it was respectf ul in tone. No one was bullie d, Mr Sio, in that process,
and no one is bullied by this bill. Dr Prasad’s constant refrain that these measures are
punitive is absolute bunkum, and I am sure deep down he knows it.
I would like to say much more on this; I will at future stages. I am proud of what we
are doing, and I really commend this bill to the House, because it is one of the most
important things we could possibly do.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: It is always good to follow Mr Macindoe on this
particular bill, the Social Security (Yout h Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill,
and indeed many others. Much of what he says does not hold up to  scrutiny at all.
Indeed, much of what the Government members have had to say on this bill does not
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2879
hold up to scrutiny at all. This is a nasty bi ll. It has nasty provisions, and it is a nasty
Government that is trying to foist this upon our most vulnerable.
There are some things we agree on. We agr ee with the Government when it says that
the best way to assist the people we are ta lking about is through work. We agree with
the Government on that, but that is where the similarities end. When Labour was in
Government it did just that. It got our mo st vulnerable into work. It reduced our
unemployment to the lowest level in the Western World. When it did that, welfare
numbers came down, people were in work, a nd people got on with it. But that side is
not creating work. Labour took an aggressive approach to creating jobs, aggressively
triaging—

items.speaker: Melissa Lee
items.text: Transferred to invalids benefits! Transferred to sickness benefits!

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: That member there who says a lot took the shortest call
possible and promptly fell asleep. Melissa Lee had better listen and argue this particular
point, because I do not know where that member was when this bill was being debated.
What this Government has done in this par ticular bill is what it has done in the ACC
area and in other areas, as well, and it is doing it now in local government reform. You
create a problem—you create the figment of a problem—then, Mr Macindoe, you apply
your own ideology. That is all this Government is doing—applying its particular
ideology. The language we hear from this Minister for Social Development is: “We will
back the young people.” If this  is backing the young people, then this is not backing at
all. To what extent is this backing young people? I shall go through it step by step and
show Mr Macindoe how that really is, indeed , intellectual dishonesty because it is not
backing young people.
The process of submissions was truncat ed—it really was tr uncated—for no good
reason. The only reason the Government ga ve was: “Oh, well, welfare reform was
introduced last year. People ha ve had their say so we need  a very short period.” What
was the Government frightened of? Was it that too many people would come and tell
members opposite that this is a bad idea? On  another bill before  the same select
committee, the Social Services Committee,  we have a long, long period of time for
submissions, and it is not as important as this  bill. It has already had other reports done.

items.speaker: But here members on that side are saying
items.text: “No, let’s truncate.”
You know, my colleague Su’a William Sio went through the submissions absolutely
honestly and religiously. I am happy to quote it back to the members opposite
absolutely and honestly. I have my notes from  the select committee. I am happy to read
them out to the members opposite. What he said was exactly what the submitters said.
Submitters did not support this bill at all—at all. I do not know where those members
opposite were, but they must have been asleep. Sam Lotu-Iiga was far too busy
managing the process and not listening to wh at people were saying, because if he had
listened, this bill would not have survived in this  form. It is a travesty. It is a travesty to
the power of a select committee. It is just not trusting our responsible citizens to come
to the select committee and make submissi ons. That side did not  hear. Can Mr Sam
Lotu-Iiga put hand on heart and say that the Government heard the submissions and has
made the changes?
Su’a William Sio: No, he can’t.

items.speaker: Dr RAJEN PRASAD
items.text: The member cannot, because th e member had instructions
from his Minister, whom they are all singi ng great praises of. I do not know who is in
for promotion next, but Todd McClay has done a travesty to his own.
Listen to the figures. There were 85 submissions, 50 opposed, nine supported, and
six were unclear. Do the ma ths. If you do that maths, it makes 73 percent who opposed
the proposal—73 percent. Applyi ng the standard of the deba cle of the class sizes, the
2880 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
Government should walk away from this bill. It should walk away from this bill,
because it has no legislative ability to do this. It has none at all.
The Government talks about taking an investment approach. An investment
approach? My big toe! There is no investment in this. If we invested in jobs, then that is
an investment approach. The marketeers have come up with a nice slogan: “Let’s use an
investment approach, let’s us e the social service language of wraparound, and we will
get there.” The Government will not get ther e, because there is no intellectual honesty
about this particular approach. This is a mean  Government. Its approach is insincere. It
is a punitive approach. It is uncharitable. It  cares little for the mo st vulnerable in our
society. That is what this Government has done.
You know, it is ironic that this Government is so hell-bent on doing so much
damage—and this bill will do damage. If th at member, Mr Macindoe, believes this will
be his finest hour, then I feel sorry for him. This cannot be his finest hour. This is going
to be quite pathetic—quite pa thetic—because there is no inve stment in this particular
approach.
Many submitters rejected the Government’s  approach to solo mothers who are
bringing up a second child. Now, after 12 mont hs, that mother has to go to work. For a
moment, Minister, turn away from the moth er and focus on the face of the child. What
does the child need? What did the child do wrong? That child needs the mother there for
as long as any mother can stay at home. But,  no, that Minister, in a nasty way, will take
that away from our young babies, and that is m ean. That is mean-spirited. What is there
about an investment approach in that? That  baby will need that mother. It is not the
baby’s fault that the baby has been born, but that is a fact. The least we can do is
support them to get the best service, to bond, and to have the time together.
It is quite ironic that this Government ta lks a lot about eviden ce. I want the next
speaker, or any member of that Government, to get up and tell me what the theory is
that actually says that this is the way to treat young people. We are taking the very tools
we have to train them, ta king their money away from them, and locking it up
somewhere. Every theory I know—and I have studied this—says that power to make
decisions shifts as the child grows older.
The independent youth benefit has been a pr oblem. Some parents have had difficulty
with this. This is the group of young people who have, really, sp lit with their own
families. Those families have not liked this benefit because, somehow, they have
blamed the benefit, but the benefit has been a response to those parents who have really
disenfranchised their own children and separa ted from them. The State has had to look
after those young people, and now those families have the ear of this Minister. They
have had the ear of this Government. They ha ve had the ear of this particular Cabinet,
because the Government is devising mean policies to ensure that they can come now
and be punitive. There is no science in this approach. People presented to us and said
that when this approach was used in Am erica, it actually increased dependency. It
actually increased it. So where is the eviden ce? Let the next speaker tell me where the
evidence is. Let the next speaker  tell me where the science is , because it is not science.
All it is is a series of punitive mechanisms.
Submitter after submitter said that this  was mean, this was bullying, this was
punitive, and this will not work. Name me one respectable organisation that submitted
and I will read the submitters out. The Human Rights Commission, the Children’s
Commissioner—they all said the same thi ng. Nine people supported this particular
measure. Mr Macindoe, by any standards, you should have the courage to say that at
least other people thought very differently.
How does this move our people further? How does this really get young people to
grow up perfectly? How does this  actually give our childre n and our babies the best
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2881
possible start in life? It doe s not. Somehow, because someone  is a beneficiary, this
Government is entitled on our behalf to be m ean to them. Well, this side will never do
that. This side will invest in the proper sense,  as indeed it has for a long time. This side
will get those people an education, will get them jobs.
Government members of that select comm ittee cannot be proud of the way in which
they conducted themselves. It was not a happy  select committee; it was a mean select
committee, and the members did not conduct th emselves well. I was not pleased to be
part of that select committee, Mr Macindoe, and I am sure that you were not, as well.
What that select committee was doing was ra ilroading, using this Minister’s directions
to you. Mr Macindoe, you and your colleagues took leave of your senses to just look at
the evidence, look at the science, and take cover. Your ideology got in the way, just like
your asset sales ideology does.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: I proudly wear this ribbon here. It is the purple
ribbon, which stands for World Elder Abuse Awareness Day. In respect of that, I will
not abuse our elderly gentleman over here, Dr Rajen Prasad, but instead I will give him
some reality. Here I stand in front of the H ouse, hand on heart, and I shall say to the
member that I in the Social Services Co mmittee heard the submissions—hand on heart.
Not only did I hear the submissions, all 21 of them—and 20 of them were written by the
Labour Party—but I heard all that they ha d to say. So there you go. To the honourable
gentleman, I say that I heard them, hand on heart. But the words that were shouted out
and ranted from over there were about th eory. I want to acknowledge the honourable
member, Rajen Prasad, as a lect urer and teacher of theory. Bu t I stand here today not as
a member of theory, but as a member of reality, because this party is the party of reality.
The member wants to hear about where the evidence is. Well, let us just say this. The
Welfare Working Group took a longitudina l study around the Ministry of Social
Development and began to see the impacts of long-term dependency on those who were
on a benefit. And what it clearly showed—here  is the reality—were the negative effects
that it had on those who are on benefits. Ho w can you argue with that ? This is reality;
this is what we are giving them. So what did we do? The honourable Minister for Social
Development, Mrs Bennett, turn ed round and said that we wa nt to deliver better public
services, we would have better choices, and we want to bring our people out of poverty.
We want a more active welfare system. That is what we want; we want a more active
welfare system. So this So cial Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment
Bill will not only modernise what is an outdated system, but will also enable this
workforce. This is a thing that, I suppose—

items.speaker: Dr Rajen Prasad
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker . It is a serious point of order.
The member has referred to a study, but he has not told us what study it was.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: No, no. Once again, that is
interrupting a member. I pulled up a Govern ment member for doing the exact thing
earlier. These are debating points.

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Thank you, Mr Speaker. This is the thing that I said. Again,
here is the point of reality, and this is what Labour members do not like. They do not
like the reality looking straight at them. And that is it, becaus e the reality is this. In the
election, with all the promises that were made  by that party, what did it do? The reality
is it lost its votes. We did not lose our votes. We gained our votes. So here is the reality.
You have become a one-trick pony. You have  kept our people in  poverty. You keep
preaching the same message—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Order!

items.speaker: ALFRED NGARO
items.text: Sorry, Mr Speaker. Labour has kept our people in poverty. That
is what it does. Why? Labour members still wa nt to say that our people need benefits.
What we are saying is that we need opportunity . That is what this bill will do, if that
2882 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
opportunity is given to us. So we sta nd here, hand on heart, and we heard the
submissions. We are no longer about theo ry—we are no longer about theory—we are
about reality, and about giving our people an op portunity so that they can see a brighter
future. Thank you.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: Is this a split call?

items.speaker: Dr Megan Woods
items.text: It is.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I call Dr Megan Woods.

items.speaker: Dr MEGAN WOODS
items.text: I am very happy to rise to speak
against the Social Security (Youth S upport and Work Focus) Amendment Bill,
especially after listening to what we have e ndured in this House tonight. We have been
told that Labour has kept its people in pove rty. We have even been misled when the
member opposite, Alfred Ngaro, put his hand ove r his heart. Well, we might like to
suggest it was covering a gap so that the wind did not whistle through. This is a serious
issue that we are facing here : to be told that Labour has kept our people in poverty.
Well, let us talk about the facts. We heard his colleague, the chair of the Social Services
Committee, talking about how National has created more jobs than ever before. Well,
here is Statistics 101—that is called population growth. The simple fact of the matter is
that there are 52 percent more unemployed people in this country than when the
members opposite took office. They should be ashamed of themselves. They have
thrown more New Zealanders on the scrap heap through their inaction and their inability
to do anything to create jobs in this country.
The reality is that there are now more than 40,000 people on the unemployment
benefit. There are 50,000 New Zealanders leav ing this country every year. If you want
to talk about taking people out of poverty, create jobs. When Labour came into office in
1992 there were 162,000 people on the unemployment benefit. By the time we left
office in 2008 there were 17,700 on the unemploymen t benefit. This is the way that you
beat poverty. We are hearing some heck ling from the members opposite about getting
real in the real world. I want to read a quote from John Key at the Job Summit, when he
launched the beginning of this brave new world and the glittering future that National
was going to offer. At the Job Summit Mr Key said: “I don’t want to spend much time
talking about how difficult economic conditions  are at the moment … I’m here to do
something about it.” Well, he has done precisely nothing except preside over an ever-
increasing dole queue, and that is not good enough.
What is more, this bill has young New Zeal anders paying for the deficit of the
Government’s thinking. Those members have  no idea how to create jobs. I want to
focus on some of the impacts on young people of this bill. In the Budget it was
trumpeted that there was going to be an upfront investment of $287.5 million over 4
years. Well, this comes at the expense of $155 million that is already committed—let us
not kid anyone here—and $58.8 million of that is being cribbed back from the Youth
Transition Services scheme, the very sche me that is there to get young people from
training and into work. We have no objection to wraparound services, but we do not see
why you would get rid of a scheme that, act ually, in many cases is being successful.
Why not build on the scheme that is already th ere? That is what we believe would have
been a far better solution. We think it is rea lly telling in places where the scheme is
working, and the obvious model was with Dale Williams in Ōtorohanga and Youth
Transition Services. The fact is that these pe ople did not even tender in the first round.
These people do not see how the new schemes being put in place are going to work. We
have zero to two young people in that area who are unemployed.
We also have huge concerns about the tendering out of the provision of these
services. We have clear evidence from Australi a, and we have clear evidence from the
United Kingdom that there is gaming of the system, and that the incentives are not there
12 Jun 2012 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill 2883
for providers to actually get young people into success. When you get paid your $1,200
bonus for getting someone to National Certific ate of Educational Achievement (NCEA)
level 2, you do not have to be a genius to wo rk out that the provide rs are going to steer
clear of the most challenging kids, many of  whom do not even have NCEA level 1. The
effort required to get them to level 2 is just going to be too immense in the time frames
they are given. This is not a bi ll that is designed to help young people. This is not a bill
that is designed to create employment. This is a bill that has young people, once again,
paying for—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member.

items.speaker: METIRIA TUREI
items.text: A great deal has been said tonight about
all of the failings of this legislation, the Social Security (Youth Support and Work
Focus) Amendment Bill, and I agree with it . I am pleased that our party, the Green
Party, is opposing this bill.
This Minister for Social Development, Paul a Bennett, uses rhetoric to disguise her
culpability in pushing more women and more children into severe poverty and hardship.
This Minister, Paula Bennett, spreads deliberate misinformation because she knows that
there is no evidence to back up these policies,  and, in fact, all the evidence shows that
they will fail women and children. This Mi nister, Paula Bennett, knows that harm will
come to women and children because of her reforms, and yet she cares nothing for the
impact on those children or their lives. Th is Minister, Paula Be nnett, is stealing the
future from those in poverty and hardship. This Minister is puni shing women for being
mothers.
We can choose a different future for our children. We can choose a different future
for all our children, rich and poor, if we c hoose to treat our children with dignity and
with justice. So I want to outline some of  the solutions that the Green Party has for
dealing with these issues, to bring women and children out of poverty.
First, research across the world proves that  educating mothers significantly increases
the well-being of their children. So for thos e who are on benefits, the first, most
important thing to do is to invest in thei r education. We will bring back the training
incentive allowance for DPB recipients, and extend it to those on sickness benefits, and
to all levels of study, so that other wome n like me and Paula Bennett, who got degrees
and got properly educated while on the benef it, are able to do so as well. And we will
extend it to sickness beneficiaries because they too should be entitled to further training
so that they can get a decent, high-level education for their future and for their kids.
We will extend the in-work tax credit to be neficiary families, because although this
Minister, Paula Bennett, cares nothing for the family of two adults and two children that
is on the benefit that has to  survive on $75 a week after re nt and food, we do care about
that family. We know, and any New Zealander li stening to this debate will agree, that
that family simply needs more money to ma ke sure that their ki ds are properly fed,
properly clothed, and properly housed. No MP in this House would ever expect
themselves or their families to have to live on $75 a week after paying rent and food.
But this Minister, Paula Bennett, cares no thing for those children in that family,
those children who are hungry and cold, and she will intenti onally discriminate against
those children. The Green Party will not discriminate. We will make Working for
Families fair for all New Zealand kids, not just those who are wealthy. We will make
sure that people are earning a decent wage when they do work. The Green Party will not
tolerate the modern-day slavery wages th at too many people—mostly women—earn in
this country. A living wage is the best next  step—to make sure that work does actually
pay—to truly bring people out of poverty. When four out of five Ne w Zealand families
have struggled to put food on th e table in the last few years,  we know that work is not a
2884 Social Security (Youth Support & Work Focus) Amdt Bill  12 Jun 2012
ladder out of poverty if wages are kept low.  This Minister and the Government she
belongs to deliberately keep wages low to keep families in poverty.
Tonight we heard from Jan Logie the stories of women living on benefits—their real,
lived experiences. We heard, in their own words, their fears for their kids, fears for their
future, and the shame that is brought upon them  by this Minister’s degradation of them
as women and mothers. Paula Bennett will force these women into work, and their
babies into day care, to punish them for ge tting pregnant. She got what she needed out
of welfare, and now she kicks the ladder out  from under her. Melissa Lee yawned when
she heard these stories of women fearful for th eir children’s future. I guess, to kick it
off, the National attitude to women might be to listen to those stories of women and
their fears for their kids, and liken them to dogs. Thank you.

items.speaker: MIKE SABIN
items.text: It is a shame that Metiria Turei’s speech
was not beamed into New Zealand households at  6 p.m., because then they might get to
really see what the Green agenda is all a bout—this absolutely ridiculous notion that
trying to support young people into work is a bout forcing them into work. Well, what
part of the equation do the Green Party and those in “Labour Land” not get? The all-are,
no-responsibility lifestyle on welfare is just not a go.
The reality is that over a period of 9 year s of Labour and the Gr eens in charge what
we actually saw was a morphing of our welfare system into a welfare trap. At its peak
some 350,000 people were beholden to the Govern ment for a benefit, at a cost of $22
million a day—$8 billion a year. It was comple tely financially unsustainable, but more
so was the human capital cost—far more. I am talking about the loss of choices, the loss
of opportunities, the lo ss of self-belief, th e loss of purpose, and the loss of hope in
individuals who were sitting th ere, beholden to a Government that at the time thought
that throwing a few crumbs at them and k eeping them beholden was a good way to stay
in office. That time has come to an end.
This Government is prepared to tackle the challenge of welfare dependency, because
we back these young people. We back these you ng people to have a lif e and to have an
opportunity, and we are putting in place the support, the mentoring, the training, the
education and the opportunities that these young people need to get their lives back on
track. We back them—and it is hard. This bill deals with deals with some 14,000 New
Zealanders, young teenage New Zealanders, 90 pe rcent of whom, in the absence of our
taking this step, will be on a collision course to  an adult benefit, and that is where they
will stay for some time, and that is unacceptable.
The Social Security (Youth Support and Work Focus) Amendment Bill is about
backing those young people, rather than leav ing them to sink or swim, because we
know that most of them will sink. This bill is about us backing our children, our young
people, with training,  childcare, education,  management of their bills, and mentoring.
This bill is about us doing what young New Z ealanders need. I commend the bill to the
House.
The question was put that the amendments  recommended by the Social Services
Committee by majority be agreed to.
A party vote was called for on the question, That the question be agreed to.
Ayes 63
New Zealand National 59; Māori Party 2; ACT New Zealand 1; United Future 1.
Noes 57

Question agreed to.

sections.heading: Exclusive Economic Zone And Continental Shelf

items.text: (ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS) BILL
Second Reading
Debate resumed from 30 May.

items.speaker: GARETH HUGHES
items.text: Kia ora. It is great to have 1 minute left to talk about
this bill, the Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects)
Bill. In the first 9 minutes of my speech on the bill I talked about all the reasons why the
Green Party is opposing this bad legislation, from the fact that  it fails our international
obligation to the fact that it prioritises  economic development over environmental
considerations. It does not pr eserve and protect our enviro nment, which is why we are
able to use our exclusive economic zone. It fails to account for climate change entirely.
It contributes to legal uncertain ty around the precauti onary principle. It is just going to
be a feeding frenzy for lawyers. It fails to meet the Treaty, fails the principles of natural
justice, and contains no marine protecti on. And although the Government has gone out
to the public, asking: “Do you want drilling to be proh ibited, discretionary, or
allowed?”, it has gone out last week and allowed 40,000 square kilometres of our ocean
to be at risk. Although we support an excl usive economic zone bill, we will not be
supporting this exclusive economic zone deep-sea drilling bill.

items.speaker: JACQUI DEAN
items.text: Why do the Greens not just come out and
say it? Why do they not just come out and say no, instead of dressing up their debate
around the Exclusive Economic Zone and Con tinental Shelf (Environmental Effects)
Bill and around various provisions of the bill ? Why do they not just come out and say
that they want to say no to anything th at means advancement for the New Zealand
economy? Why do they not just say it? Why do they not just use a little frankness and
openness in this House,  and say what they really thin k? Why do they not use a little
“frack-ness”—frankness—and say what they really think, which is that on anything that
advances the economic well-being of New Zeal and and is to do with the environment,
they are just going to say no?
Well, in fact, this Exclusive Economic Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental
Effects) Bill does a number of things. What it does is fill a regulatory gap that currently
exists in New Zealand regulation. Outside in the exclusive economic zone currently
there is no regulatory framework for activit ies that occur in the exclusive economic
zone area. Yes, we do have the Maritime Transport Act and we also have the Health and
Safety in Employment Act, which provide some environmental protections out in the
exclusive economic zone, but we do not have currently a framework for regulations and
marine consents. That is what this bill does.
Why the Greens could possibly be against a bill that provides for frameworks for
regulations and marine consen ts quite frankly is beyond me, but I am sure they will
have another opportunity to put their case to Parliament. What this bill does is provide
for independent decision-making from the E nvironmental Protection Authority. It also
gives effect—and this is, again, where I disa gree with the view of  the Green Party and,
2886 EEZ & Continental Shelf (Environmental Effects) Bill 12 Jun 2012
indeed, the Labour Party—to our internationa l obligations. It is most important to
remember—I recall a contribution from a La bour member in the previous time when
this bill was debated—that this  bill is not about oil spill response. This is not about
mineral allocation or marine reserves. This bill is not about fishing.
During the course of the Local Governme nt and Environment Committee scrutiny of
this bill, a number of discussions were heard around the Resource Management Act and
why it was that the principles  of the Resource Management Act were used for part of
this bill and for part of this bill were not  used. We received some pretty good advice on
that, and I just want to go over it because, for some reason, again, some Labour
members seem to be suddenly very fond of the Resource Management Act, and feel that
it should be the piece of legislation that is given effect to in the Exclusive Economic
Zone and Continental Shelf (Environmental Ef fects) Bill. But there are several reasons
why it should not be. There are areas of th e Resource Management  Act that are not
applicable to the bill, and th at is because of the differe nt regulatory context of the
Resource Management Act and what is happe ning in the exclusive economic zone area.
I guess, for practical reasons, there would be provisions describing restrictions on—

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I am sorry to interrupt the
honourable member. The time has come for me to leave the Chair.
Debate interrupted.
